Man Buys New 2023 Chevy Corvette Z06 Convertible for $156,400, Drives 6k Miles, Sells for $103,000
15 photos
Photo: Bring a Trailer
I'm not here to tell you what to like or not like. But C8 specs such as this one are more of an acquired taste. Still, in a vacuum, this Z06 Convertible was a steal at just $103,000. It cost its original owner $156,400 when new, and it's only done roughly 6,000 miles. It's not next to nothing, but it's not tragic either.
Value-wise, this hits the sweet spot for me. It's that "little over $100k" figure that feels just right for a used C8 Z06, if your goal is simply put, bang for your buck. I would gladly take on an even higher mileage example if it meant a more conventional spec at the same price. Then again, I don't really mind the exterior on this car that much.
The "problem" I have is that it looks custom, so what I'd do is remove all the red vinyl wrap accents, including that custom Stingray logo on the hood/frunk. There's already enough red on the inside. We don't need any more of it on the outside. I'd also ditch the chrome on the factory 20" and 21" wheels. The car is already bright enough. As for the interior, not much you can do there - I guess you just have to live with it and hopefully not get a headache every time you get behind the wheel.
Let's take a closer look at the spec, though, starting with the exterior. Since it's a convertible, this Vette also comes with a power-retractable hardtop. Then you've got the rear wing, dive planes, ground effects, nacelles and mirror caps - all finished in Carbon Flash; while the grille insert is trimmed in carbon fiber. Other goodies include the LED headlights, black exhaust outlets, and the front-axle lift system.
Since this has the Z07 Performance Package, it means it gets the Z07 suspension and braking system, featuring Bright Red-painted Brembo calipers over carbon-ceramic rotors.
Meanwhile, inside is where you'll find the Adrenaline Red Dipped leather upholstery, power-adjustable GT2 bucket seats, color-coordinated... everything (as in the dash, center console, door panels, carpets, seat belts); plus the likes of a 14-speaker Bose Performance Series sound system, a Performance Data and Video recorder, wireless charging for your mobile device, Apple CarPlay and Android Auto connectivity, a carbon fiber and leather-trimmed steering wheel, and more.
Photo: Bring a Trailer There are no surprises here when it comes to performance. There's a 5.5-liter LT6 V8 engine pushing 670 horsepower and 460 lb-ft of torque to the rear wheels via a Tremec TR-9080 eight-speed dual-clutch automatic. The car came factory-fitted with a performance exhaust with driver-selectable modes.
In a straight line, the Z06 Convertible can rocket to 60 mph (97 kph) in 2.6 seconds (with a 1-foot rollout). In this particular case, since the car is equipped with the Z07 package , the top speed is "only" 189 mph (304 kph), instead of the usual 195 mph (314 kph).

The U.S. Department of Transportation announced $2.3 billion for 105 freight and passenger rail projects in 45 states and Washington, D.C., including bridge repairs, track upgrades, and port connections.
What’s Related
The projects will improve more than 2,000 miles of track and receive an additional $1.9 billion in state, local and private funding. Together, those contributions bring total funding to more than $4.2 billion.
The Federal Railroad Administration selected the projects through its Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements program, known as CRISI. The awards include work on shortline railroads, freight yards, and passenger routes.
“The funds announced today will provide shortline railroads across the country with the resources they need to make long overdue improvements to their day-to-day operations,” said FRA Administrator David Fink.
RELATED STORIES: DOT Awards $200 Million to Expand Truck Parking Across 12 States | Amazon Adds Direct Rail Route From Los Angeles to the East Coast
Projects receiving funding
Among the projects selected:
$33.6 million for Arkansas & Missouri Railroad: Replace rail and ties between Fort Smith, Arkansas, and Monett, Missouri, add two siding tracks, and upgrade an existing siding so trains can enter or leave from either end. The project also includes equipment to reduce rail wear on sharp curves.
$43.5 million for Wheeling & Lake Erie Railway in Ohio: Rehabilitate eight of the Toledo Swing Bridge’s 11 spans over the Maumee River and replace timber fender systems. The work will allow the bridge to handle railcars weighing 286,000 pounds.
$37 million for the Maine Department of Transportation: Rehabilitate about 90 miles of railroad in northern Maine by replacing rail, ties and ballast and repairing a railroad bridge deck.
$20 million for Aberdeen Carolina & Western Railway in North Carolina : Install approximately 30 miles of continuous welded rail, repair bridges, and upgrade crossing signals in Montgomery and Stanly counties.
$30 million for Texas City Terminal Railway : Rehabilitate and expand its rail yard and realign a port vehicle entrance. DOT said the work will address a conflict between trains and vehicles entering a petroleum facility and help handle petrochemical exports.
$218 million for the Wisconsin Department of Transportation: Extend Chicago–Milwaukee Hiawatha passenger service to Waukesha, Jefferson, and Dane counties. The project includes track, bridge, and crossing improvements, along with new passenger stations.
Demand exceeded available funding
FRA received 368 applications seeking approximately $12.2 billion, more than five times the amount awarded. The agency evaluated applications based on project readiness, technical merit, and expected benefits.
The selections cover projects at different stages, including planning, design, and construction. Construction and completion schedules will vary by project.
“From improving shortline infrastructure and port connections so critical products can get where they need to go faster to enhancing fencing along trespassing hotspots, this package will tangibly improve lives for millions of Americans,” said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

RoleyX Bond S10 Is a Flagship E-Scooter From a New Chinese Brand – Coming in Hot at $1,200
17 photos
Photo: RoleyX
With each passing day, it seems that there’s a new e-scooter brand popping up and frankly, that’s kind of the case. This time around, we explore one such crew and what they promise to bring to the table.
If you type in “RoleyX” in a Google search bar, the first result you’ll get is “Rolex,” as if this omnipotent search engine has no idea who RoleyX may be. That’s how new this crew is, with the name hitting the scene in mid to late 2026. Currently, they only offer one unit, and that’s what we’re here to explore.
It’s called the Bond S10, and while it may not have anything to do with the film franchise, nor do I know what that S10 stands for, it is this brand’s first e-scooter , or the proverbial flagship, the one that’s meant to showcase what this name is all about.
Photo: RoleyX First and foremost, the S10 is currently up for grabs at no more than $1,200 (€1,100), placing it in the low to middle range in terms of what the market offers, and if I may, it actually brings in some value. There have also been people that said “yes” to this two-wheeler, and for the time being, the S10 does carry a 4.9/5.0-star rating.
One reason why folks are liking this one has a whole lot to do with speed, which is set at a peak of 40 mph (64 kph) out of the box, so plenty of kick to ensure that you can leave the car at home, if only for a few miles each week. Maybe e-scooters are your chosen means of transport.
This top speed is granted by the presence of two motors, with 1,000 W a piece as nominal. However, there is a mention of a peak of 3,200 W on the manufacturer’s website, but it’s not clear if this is per motor, or both together. I’m banking on the latter because 6,400 W would place this one in the hyper scooter range, and it isn’t.
Do note that another section of the product page does mention a peak output of 3,500 W, which is roughly 4.7 hp. Oh, and some riders have reported a top speed that sits higher than 40 mph, so there’s a bit more power than we’re told.
Photo: RoleyX These two motors are also strong enough to help riders up hills with an incline of as much as 35%, which is very good for something in this price range and more than enough pull to ensure some punchy acceleration. The latter stands at a 0-30 mph (0-48 kph) time in under four seconds.
The S10 is also built upon a 52 V ecosystem, accounting for that acceleration. Be sure to have some knowledge of how to ride an e-scooter before playing around with the fastest mode.
One very strong point for the S10 is range, rolling in with a peak of 65 miles (105 km), made possible by a 20 Ah battery mounted into the deck. Clearly, the faster we ride, the less range we can expect, but from my own experience, we can see around 50% of what manufacturers mention zipping around our cities with mixed speed settings.
What I liked about this fresh brand is that they do tell riders what we can expect from rides at full speed; just 16 miles can be accessed if you ride at a constant 40 mph. Once we’re out of juice, it takes up to 10 hours before being able to ride again.
Photo: RoleyX RoleyX does state that their e-scooter carries an IPX6 rating and does show it moving around through puddles and all that, made possible by a patented system and a BMS. Another feature that protects the battery is the frame itself, completed from forged aluminum to resist torsional forces.
Yet, speed means nothing without control, and to ensure that you stay on top of things, literally, a C-arm suspension is called upon, a tried and tested system that countless EV of this style calls upon. Hydraulic shocks are used for damping and rebound, and can handle riders as large as 256 lbs (120 kg).
Allow me to point out that this sort of suspension is one that does allow riders to break away from the tarmac and tackle hardpack roads and even some dirt trails . There are clear limits to e-scooter though, so ride responsibly.
More softness and control are granted by the 10-inch tires with 3.0-inch cross-section. They are pneumatic and tubeless and carry a hybrid tread that will clearly keep you riding fast on tarmac but let us tap into those light off-road settings I mentioned. Rubber compound is also an often-overlooked aspect that contributes to stopping times, so be sure to explore other options out there if the standard ones aren’t to your liking.
Photo: RoleyX In this price range, most brands also integrated hydraulic brakes into the mix and for the S10, this is true too. A pair of oil-activated pistons clamp down on 5.5-inch rotors at the front and rear.
Toss on a display with NFC unlock, ambient lighting in the stem, deck, a headlight ad taillight, and we’re almost done. Almost because the S10 also carries a geometry that’s designed to keep the handlebar as stable as possible at high speeds.
I didn’t make out whether or not the S10 has a steering damper, but RoleyX does showcase a rider rolling around with one hand on the handlebar and the other holding a phone up to his ear. Some sources do mention that there is a steering damper at play too.
From where I'm standing, the S10 is looking pretty good, with real riders claiming the same. Ride safe out there; gear up properly.

A Dallas court has upheld the $604 million damages award against C.H. Robinson in a fatal truck crash case, turning July’s advisory jury verdict into a judgment against the freight broker.
What’s Related
The ruling leaves the damages and the jury’s allocation of fault unchanged in Lipe v. Lupus Superior. The lawsuit alleged that C.H. Robinson negligently selected an unsafe carrier before a fatal March 2021 truck accident in Mississippi.
The jury assigned 45% of the fault to the driver, 32% to carrier Lupus Superior and 23% to C.H. Robinson. The court also held the broker responsible for the driver’s share, bringing its responsibility to 68%, Moore wrote.
That finding put C.H. Robinson above the 50% threshold for joint and several liability under Texas law, making it answerable for the full award. The company disputes the judgment and plans to appeal.
RELATED: C.H. Robinson Agrees to Buy RXO in $5.8 Billion Cash-and-Stock Deal
C.H. Robinson strongly disagrees
Dorothy Capers, C.H. Robinson’s chief legal officer, told Logistics Management that the company strongly disagrees with the judgment and remains confident in its appeal.
“Nothing about our rejection of the judgment diminishes the profound loss suffered by the families in this case,” Capers said. “But C.H. Robinson did not cause or contribute to the accident, and accountability must be grounded in the facts and the law.”
Capers said the carrier had safely delivered nearly 270 loads for C.H. Robinson customers and held a satisfactory federal safety rating when selected and after a federal review of the accident. She called for a national standard for evaluating carrier safety.
Importance of carrier ratings
According to the Transportation Intermediaries Association (TIA), Lupus Superior exceeded intervention thresholds in two federal safety measurement categories that could place it among carriers prioritized for investigation.
TIA President and CEO Chris Burroughs said in July that the carrier had maintained a satisfactory Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) rating since 2014, reaffirmed in 2021 and again this past April. He said jurors received information about the carrier’s prior incidents and safety record that brokers could not access.
“To that end, TIA has formally petitioned FMCSA to establish a clear motor carrier selection standard and to make the so-called ‘high-risk’ carrier list publicly available,” Burroughs said.
Analyst expects a reduction on appeal
Moore said the court’s ruling relied on findings that made C.H. Robinson responsible for the driver’s conduct, including a finding that the driver was a borrowed employee. He expects an appeal to reduce the award.
“We continue to believe the borrowed-employee finding was unlikely to survive judicial scrutiny and that the award is likely to be materially reduced on appeal,” Moore wrote.

Photo: Zum
A fleet of 74 school buses have spent the last two years powering about a thousand homes, taking stress off the grid, thanks to V2G chargers built in America.
If you’ve spent much time around the electric vehicle space, you may have heard about vehicle-to-grid, perhaps by the acronym V2G (or its cousins, V2H/V2L/V2X, etc).
The basic idea is: if we’re looking to add batteries to the grid or to homes to increase stability and smooth out demand, why don’t we use the massive amounts of batteries available inside electric vehicles for that purpose?
The idea has been talked about for years, but for the most part has not reached wide adoption. The California Energy Commission estimates that V2H could save homeowners a few hundred dollars per summer, and cut peak demand by up to 5GW statewide if it was broadly implemented. But to do this with consumer EVs, homes would mostly need some sort of costly equipment added, and most EVs aren’t V2G-enabled (though that may be changing ).
Advertisement - scroll for more content
But for fleet EVs, installation can be a lot easier. Putting V2G in homes requires a lot of small scale projects, distributed across a region. But putting V2G in a fleet location lets you access a lot of batteries in one big project, and lets you aggregate those batteries more easily.
So that’s exactly what Tellus Power, a charging equipment manufacturer in Irvine, CA, is doing. We took a tour of its facility and met with CEO Mike Calise and CTO Srikanth Kanaparthi.
The company has been building AC and DC chargers (up to 480kW) since 2010, but its newest push is into V2G chargers, particularly for fleets. It assembles them in America, and they’re “Build America Buy America” compliant.
Its first project in this push was an installation of V2G chargers for Oakland, CA’s school district, covering 74 school buses. The chargers were built by Tellus, and the project is operated by Zum. We first wrote about the Oakland project in 2024 , but now we have a couple years of data to show how it’s going.
Collectively, the buses have a total of 11.5MWh of energy storage. Buses fill up overnight, use about 20-40% of their charge during the day, then plug in to V2G chargers after the school day and discharge to feed the grid, just in time for the late afternoon rush on electricity, when people get home and turn on air conditioning, start cooking, turn on the lights and so on.
Or on holidays and summertime (when the grid is the most stressed in California), they can be a grid resource all day long.
74 buses may not sound like much, but with the amount of energy available on board and the total power output of the chargers, it can fuel a lot of houses. The fleet can discharge at about 2 Megawatts at once, and each house uses about 2 kilowatts on average in the evening (though that can spike higher due to HVAC/EV use). That means, altogether, this fleet of 74 buses can power around a thousand homes.
Over the course of the last two years, the bus fleet has returned a total of 1.7GWh of energy to the grid, and has had over 99.5% uptime. This basically turns the fleet into a small and reliable peaker plant, which has delivered on the order of hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of electricity to the grid over the last couple years.
Tellus says V2G capacity can get onto the grid faster than any other kind of power plant. A fleet V2G depot can take months to deploy, compared to a timeline of years to build and attach other power plants to the grid. And Tellus says that its chargers differ from others on the market in that they don’t require large transformers on-site, which makes deployment faster and less expensive.
V2G isn’t strictly a “power plant,” since it’s not generating electricity. But it does shift supply to when it’s needed most, which is also when it’s most expensive. This “energy arbitrage” lets Oakland school district buy power when it’s cheap and sell it when it’s expensive, which makes money.
That’s Tellus’ oldest project, but there are others in place and being built – 4 school buses in Burlington, VT; 2 city bus chargers for Lynch Bus Lines in Burnaby, British Columbia, Canada; a pilot program at 3 school district sites for ComEd in Illinois; and a fleet of 104 school buses (scaling to 238) in San Francisco, CA.
But even though buses are a popular choice for V2G , there are plenty of other municipal vehicles that are ripe for electrification, which have similar duty cycles and could be used for grid services.
Trash trucks are an obvious one, and they’re the next direction Tellus would like to go in. There are a number of electric garbage trucks out there, and they could generate revenue to offset costs in the same way that school buses can.
All of this together offers a large revenue opportunity for fleets, whether those fleets be private or public. If you have a bunch of vehicles, running those vehicles off of batteries can both save you money on fuel (especially with oil prices being at all-time highs ) and generate revenue with grid services, if you install V2G chargers.

More than six in 10 Gen Z apparel shoppers have bought multiple sizes or styles intending to keep just one, according to Locus Robotics . That compares with 15% of Baby Boomers, pointing to a sharp generational divide in buying habits that creates additional returns work for retailers .
What’s Related
The practice, known as “bracketing,” was also reported by 52% of Millennials and 37% of Gen X shoppers. The findings measure whether respondents have bracketed a purchase, not how often they do it.
Younger shoppers are also buying products soon after discovering them on social media, according to the report. That can leave retailers responding to sudden demand spikes while processing returns and getting merchandise ready to sell again.
RELATED STORIES: Gen Z Isn’t Sold on Supply Chain Careers—But It’s Not Too Late | Can Gen Z Solve the Truck Driver Shortage?
Extra work for retailers
Bracketing puts returns into the purchasing decision before an order reaches the customer. For retailers, that means some shipped merchandise is likely to come back, adding inspection, sorting and restocking work.
Those tasks compete for time and resources with picking and shipping new orders. Getting returned merchandise ready for resale also matters when another shopper is looking for the same size or style.
“Retail fulfillment operators are facing an entirely new reality, where demand patterns can change in hours and days, not seasons,” said Rick Faulk, CEO of Locus Robotics.
Influence of social media
Among Gen Z respondents, 79% had purchased an apparel, beauty or skincare product after discovering it on social media. The figure was 75% for Millennials and 26% for Baby Boomers.
More than two-thirds of those buyers made their purchase within three days of discovery. According to Locus, that short window can create demand spikes as products gain online attention.
The company argues that these shifts strengthen the case for warehouse automation that can adjust to changing order volumes and tasks. The consumer survey, however, examines shopping behavior rather than comparing the performance of different fulfillment approaches.
Availability of item is crucial
An unavailable item, size, shade, or formula caused 33% of shoppers to abandon or delay a purchase, the most frequently cited reason in the study. Meanwhile, 17% said they require same- or next-day delivery.
Physical stores accounted for 48% of respondents’ most recent purchases in the categories studied, making them the most frequently used purchase channel overall. Retailers must meet that in-store demand alongside online orders and returns.
“We’re seeing this firsthand with a record number of peak robot requests to help retailers around the world respond to demand surges,” Faulk said.
The findings are based on a survey of 1,000 U.S. adults about purchase frequency, shopping channels, delivery expectations, and returns behavior. The study focused on apparel, beauty, and skincare.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that decisions taken by the United States on the war in Ukraine, including delays in arms shipments and restrictions on intelligence sharing, were “hard to explain.”
“Because it all comes down to (Russian President Vladimir) Putin’s refusal to end this war, and to decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends,” Zelenskyy said in a meeting with a U.S. congressional delegation.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine had not received full explanations over limitations placed on the use of the Starshield system needed to stage some drone strikes and defend against Russian attacks, particularly by high-speed jet-powered drones.
In remarks posted on a video on Telegram, he said that on three occasions in the past week, Ukraine had not received the advance warning of an attack generally provided by its partners.
“We also know that, unfortunately, the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that our partner have already paid for through the PURL programme,” he said.
He said that to his knowledge one missile package was waiting for signature by U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
“All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us,” he said.
Affected by the U.S. delays are urgently needed Patriot interceptor missiles, just as Russia has intensified its targeting of Ukrainian cities with missiles and drones, the Washington Post reported .
Zelenskyy also said that Ukraine was willing to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, as demanded by U.S. President Donald Trump, for 30 days if Washington supplied Ukraine with interceptors for the Patriot anti-missile system.
He also said that he hoped a Ukrainian delegation would meet in the coming days with U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Norway.

Astrolab Lander At HPE Discover 2026 Large
HPE has announced that its Spaceborne Computer-4 will power artificial intelligence workloads and, according to it, will be the first HPC benchmark on the lunar surface. The compute module is set to ride aboard Astrolab’s FLIP rover, which will land near the Moon’s South Pole as part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative. This moves HPE’s spaceborne program beyond the International Space Station and into an atmosphere-free environment with much higher radiation exposure.
The mission is intended to launch in late 2026 on Voyager Technologies’ Griffin-1 lander. Once deployed, Spaceborne Computer-4 will run large language model retrieval-augmented generation, vision inference, LiDAR data processing for mapping and navigation, and an AI services container designed to demonstrate reliable deployment of scalable AI applications at the lunar edge. AI is headed to the moon.
Astrolab HPE Spaceborne 4 CA Photo 1
We first covered this hardware in June, when we looked inside the storage of Spaceborne Computer-4 at HPE Discover. The fourth iteration is a much smaller and lighter system than the HPE Spaceborne Computer-1 we covered years ago, which makes sense because mass is critical when sending payloads to the Moon. The idea is to build a small compute subsystem that can operate with low mass, low power, and that can make decisions locally, rather than having to transmit back to Earth.
The Spaceborne Computer-4 is a compact, fanless compute module built for the lunar environment
Since there is no air on the Moon to move across a heatsink, the system uses a space radiator instead of fans. The housing has an intricate lattice structure that we saw in person at Discover 2026.
The front of the compute module shows its compact, self-contained design
For storage, the system uses a Kioxia BG-series M.2 SSD , the same class of DRAM-less drive you might find in a low-cost TinyMiniMicro PC. Kioxia has been proving commercial NAND on the ISS for years, and this mission extends that work to the Moon’s harsher radiation environment.
The module’s construction is designed to survive launch vibration and the lunar thermal environment
HPE says the compute module is lightweight, self-contained, fanless, and equipped with both a low-power CPU and GPU. The company also assembled software to optimize interaction with Earth-based resources and securely deliver results back from the Moon.
The module is light enough to be lifted by hand, which matters for lunar payload mass budgets
HPE will also support Astrolab’s mission control in Hawthorne, California, using HPE Private Cloud and HPE CloudOps Software to manage and automate workloads from Earth.
The bottom of the compute module shows its mounting plate and construction
NASA and Deloitte are joining the mission to deploy additional AI workloads. NASA will run its FLUID (Federated Learning for Unbounded and Intelligent Decentralization) experiment, coordinating three separate AI models trained on data from Earth, the Moon, and the International Space Station. NASA will also conduct a tuned LLM test with semantic processing abilities to search and interpret onboard documents. Deloitte’s Silent Shield system will provide near real-time predictive cyber-analytics and anomaly detection.
Astrolab HPE Spaceborne 4 CA Photo 2
We missed an event in Hawthorne, CA last week due to OCP 2026, but we received a few photos from the event.
Final Words
If these benchmarks work as planned, they will provide useful data on whether off-the-shelf-class components can support the emerging lunar economy instead of requiring expensive custom space-grade silicon. We expect this compute mission to succeed, assuming it powers on on the lunar surface. Given the cost of lunar launches, everything is thoroughly tested before it gets loaded into a rocket.

Gilead’s emvistegrast delivered greater clinical response than placebo, setting up the asset for Phase 3 testing in ulcerative colitis as well as studies in other inflammatory diseases and bolstering the company’s push beyond its HIV portfolio.
Gilead Sciences’ investigational drug emvistegrast delivered higher response rates versus placebo in a Phase 2 study of ulcerative colitis—findings that analysts at BMO Capital Markets say “validate” the pharma’s efforts to diversify beyond HIV and into immunology and inflammation.
“Gilead’s asset looks highly competitive vs other a4b7 agents,” BMO wrote in a note on Monday. The group pointed to Eli Lilly’s zotemtegrast and Takeda’s Entyvio, which similarly block the a4b7 integrin in order to suppress inflammation in the gut.
In the mid-stage SWIFT trial, 238 patients with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis were randomly assigned to receive 200 mg, 75 mg or 25 mg of oral emvistegrast daily or placebo. Results, presented Monday at the 2025 United European Gastroenterology Week in Barcelona, Spain, showed that 66% of patients on the highest dose of emvistegrast achieved clinical response, compared to 37% of patients on placebo.
The treatment benefit was nominally significant, meeting the study’s primary endpoint. Clinical response rates for the 75-mg and 25-mg doses of emvistegrast were 51% and 43%, respectively, according to Gilead’s presentation at the conference.
With these data, Gilead plans to take emvistegrast into late-stage development—a Phase 3 study set to start next year—with an eye toward future emvistegrast combination therapies, said Swati Tole, senior vice president of Clinical Development, Inflammation, in a prepared statement.
Gilead is also looking to launch a Phase 2b/3 study of the asset in Crohn’s disease, noted BMO, which also flagged the company’s plans to test emvistegrast in combination with other assets, both internal and external, for inflammatory bowel disease.
“Taken together, we view SWIFT as an incremental positive for Gilead’s inflammatory strategy that establishes emvistegrast as a credible oral a4b7 option,” the analysts wrote.
Like BMO, analysts at Truist Securities “view the 200 mg cohort results as competitive,” they told investors on Monday. However, the firm pointed out that “dose response is not perfect,” particularly in terms of secondary endpoints. Rates of clinical remission, for instance, reached 31% in the highest dose group, but came out to 9% and 20% in the 75-mg and 25-mg arms, respectively. Remission in placebo was 8%.
A similar pattern emerged for the other secondary endpoints—including mucosal healing, endoscopic improvement and histologic endoscopic mucosal improvement—with “75 mg underperforming 25 mg,” Truist explained. Gilead chalked up the lack of a dose response effect to “potential study noise” and small treatment arm sizes, the analysts wrote after speaking with Tole and other members of the Gilead team. The pharma hasn’t yet provided a mechanistic explanation for this discrepancy, Truist flagged.
“Despite an uneven dose response, we see the data as encouraging clinical POC [proof of concept] for emvistegrast and another step in GILD’s broader I&I ambitions,” Truist noted. Indeed, Gilead’s business is heavily reliant on its HIV portfolio, which in the second quarter accounted for $5.7 billion of the company’s total $7.8 billion sales.
Seeking to diversify , Gilead has recently struck multiple deals beyond its infectious disease comfort zone. In February, for instance, the pharma dropped $7.8 billion to swallow its CAR T collaborator Arcellx ahead of a key decision for the partners’ investigational multiple myeloma therapy anitocabtagene autoleucel (anito-cel). The asset is under review with a decision expected by Dec. 23.
Other pickups in Gilead’s diversification drive this year include the inflammatory biotech Ouro Medicines and the antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) developer Tubulis , with which the bigger company had previously partnered and which will operate as an ADC specialist under the Gilead umbrella. Gilead last week also secured an equity stake in Vir Biotechnology, giving its vote of confidence to the biotech’s T cell engager platform. The pharma put up to $1.74 billion on the line in milestones, and in return received three dual-masked T cell engagers that it plans to study for solid tumors.

TraceLink is offering a $1 million winner-takes-all prize to the individual or team that builds the best AI -powered business process using its OPUS supply chain software . The global competition will launch in January 2027 and is open to developers, companies, business process specialists and university teams.
What’s Related
The OPUS Agentic Business Process Challenge asks participants to build and demonstrate a working process that addresses a business problem. Entries will use AI agents, software that can carry out tasks, alongside people, company systems and business rules to handle work that requires coordination across systems and organizations.
Participants do not need an existing paid relationship with TraceLink or a company sponsor. Beginning in January, they will receive access to OPUS Link Labs, the company’s development environment, along with training and development resources.
TraceLink introduced the competition at its FutureLink Barcelona event, which runs October 19–21. The company plans to release eligibility rules, judging criteria, technical requirements, and submission instructions before the January launch.
What participants will build
The challenge focuses on what TraceLink calls “Agentic Business Processes.” These bring multiple AI agents together with people and business systems to complete a broader process, rather than handling only an individual task.
For supply chain work, that can involve coordinating actions between different organizations and systems within a company. TraceLink says OPUS provides tools to organize those steps, connect data and give agents the business information and rules they need to do their work.
The company describes OPUS as a no-code platform, meaning participants can build processes without writing traditional software code. Entries must demonstrate a working process, so participants will need to show how their ideas function in practice.
Who can enter and what comes next
TraceLink is inviting software developers, AI engineers, process automation specialists, business process architects and consultants to participate. Companies can also enter, including customers, systems integrators, consulting firms and technology providers, while universities and academic teams are welcome.
One winning individual or team will receive the full $1 million award. TraceLink may also showcase selected submissions, although the announcement does not specify a submission deadline, an award date, or how entries will be scored.
The company says the competition is intended to encourage more people to learn OPUS and demonstrate the range of business processes that can be built with it.
“We believe the opportunity to transform business processes with AI agents is far greater than the market recognizes today,” said Shabbir Dahod, president and CEO of TraceLink.

Emerald Horizon plans to sell a hybrid battery and molten-salt storage system now and add an accelerator-driven thorium generator later. The generator remains at an early stage of development.
Austria decided against nuclear power in the late 1970s and has not revisited the question since, according to Mario Müller, vice president of research and development (R&D) at Emerald Horizon AG . Even so, the Graz-based start-up now wants to sell a thorium-fueled machine that fits in shipping containers and runs only while a particle accelerator drives it.
Founded in 2019 and listed on the Vienna Stock Exchange in June this year, Emerald Horizon calls its system SMRX, short for subcritical micromodular reactor. The company says the X stands for its approach and technology: a “neXt generation” of energy production, an “Xternal” neutron source, and an “Xcelerator,” a nod to the accelerators used to generate neutrons in modern cancer treatment, a principle the company says it applies to generating energy. It describes the system as combining energy storage and generation, which is its tagline.
The system has two parts. The first, DUALstorePLUS, is a storage system the company expects to have available as soon as this year, battery units first and molten-salt units in 2028. The second, ADES (accelerator-driven energy source), is a thorium generator that the company’s website says will reach prototype completion in 2029. The company’s materials place ADES at technology readiness level (TRL) 4.5 on a nine-point scale. They describe the integrated system as not yet demonstrated, with the remaining work in integration, commissioning, and scale-up. In a written response, the company told POWER it is targeting a demonstration plant in 2031, followed by serial production. It said many development steps run in parallel rather than one after another, and that from its perspective today, regulation will be the most important challenge.
In an interview with POWER , Florian Wagner, Emerald Horizon’s CEO, said the design is meant to answer the objections that have dogged nuclear power in his home country. “Austria is extremely against nuclear,” he said.
Storage First
The commercial plan is sequenced around cash flow. DUALstorePLUS pairs a battery container with a molten-salt thermal store, both controlled by an artificial intelligence (AI)-based master control unit. According to company materials, the battery side is roughly 5 MWh of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) per module, with about 94% roundtrip efficiency. The thermal side is 5 MWh(th) of solar salt (a mixture of potassium nitrate [KNO 3 ] and sodium nitrate [NaNO 3 ]) per module, operating between 200C and 550C. A system can be configured from 5 MWh to 100 MWh, with up to 10 modules of each type.
Wagner said the company buys the battery containers from the market, which he described as removing development risk. The molten-salt unit, called CALstore, is the company’s own design. Wagner said its prototype is running and moving toward serial production, and Müller said it has been transferred to the Netherlands for industrial reproduction. Emerald Horizon said battery energy storage system deliveries could begin as early as the fourth quarter of 2026. It expects CALstore will be available from 2028. Müller said the thermal unit can hold heat at 550C for up to 14 days.
Emerald Horizon intends to lease the DUALstorePLUS units under 20-year energy-as-a-service contracts rather than sell them. Wagner said the arrangement gives the company early revenue while the generator is developed, and gives it two to three years to build customer relationships and connect storage to grids, heat networks, or industrial processes before generation arrives. The company has not yet offered energy-as-a-service contracts to any potential SMRX customers, but it said “numerous” nondisclosure agreements with interested parties have been signed.
How ADES Is Meant to Work
ADES replaces the self-sustaining chain reaction of a conventional reactor with an external neutron source. According to the company, that source is an accelerator, and a component called the X-Amplifier Box connects it to the thorium loop (Figure 1) and amplifies the neutron flux. The company said that when the accelerator is switched off, the reaction stops. The neutrons strike thorium dissolved in a circulating fluoride salt. The salt serves as both fuel carrier and heat-transfer fluid, and heat exchangers pass the energy to a converter that can produce electricity, hydrogen, or process heat.
1. This illustration shows Emerald Horizon’s approach, utilizing an accelerator and X-amplifier in the process. Courtesy: Emerald Horizon AG
“When you activate the accelerator, you get heat back, and when you’re not activated, nothing happens,” Wagner said. The company’s materials specify an effective neutron multiplication factor below one, meaning the reaction does not sustain itself.
Müller said the engineering question now under study is how close to criticality the system can run while remaining safe. The second question is how to keep the energy release stable. The company is working in simulation, using Monte Carlo codes for neutron transport and multiphysics models for salt heating, heat flux, and loop dynamics, followed by progressively larger functional models. Müller said a 1-MW molten-salt loop is being built in the Netherlands and will be completed next year, to demonstrate pumps, heat exchangers, and salt handling at megawatt-scale heat transfer. The company said in a written response that more than 70% of the mechanical testing of ADES has been completed, owing to work on CALstore.
One ADES module is rated at 25 MW thermal and roughly 10 MW electric. The company says it needs no refueling for 20 years, after which the 40-foot container holding the salt loop would be swapped out. Müller likened it to “a cartridge.” The company states a design target of converting roughly 80% of the fuel into usable energy and says the system produces virtually no transuranic waste, with the remaining waste consisting mainly of fission products with relatively short half-lives. However, those are design targets, not demonstrated results.
Why Thorium, and Why Now
Müller said thorium was sidelined during the Cold War because uranium reactors can also supply weapons material. Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s molten-salt reactor program was aimed at developing a breeder reactor that would run on the thorium–uranium-233 fuel cycle, though the Molten-Salt Reactor Experiment the lab operated from 1965 to 1969 ran on uranium-235 and later uranium-233. Müller added that corrosion, long the obstacle for molten salts, can now be managed with redox control of the salt chemistry and with nickel alloys such as Inconel.
Wagner said the company’s timing bet was on accelerators. When the concept took shape about nine years ago, he said, Emerald Horizon wagered that more powerful accelerators would become available. “This is exactly now,” he said. Current accelerators are not yet powerful enough to fit in a single container with the required output, he acknowledged, so early units may use two or three accelerator containers. Wagner said first-generation modules might deliver closer to 7 MW electric than 10 MW. He said the full-power version would follow the prototype by about 18 months.
Built Like a Product
Emerald Horizon’s central claim is that it is building a machine, not a plant. “What we’re building is not a nuclear power plant, we’re building a machine,” Müller said. Wagner said the containers can be produced “like a car or a truck in a factory.”
The manufacturing partner is VDL Groep, a Dutch industrial conglomerate having more than 13,500 employees. According to Emerald Horizon, VDL completed a five-month due diligence and confirmed co-development and manufacturing on April 30, 2025, and VDL would build the first SMRX factory at its own site. VDL supplies another Dutch company, ASML, whose lithography machines chipmakers use to print their most advanced microchips; ASML says it is the only supplier able to produce the extreme ultraviolet (EUV) version of that equipment. Wagner acknowledged that the accelerator makes the design more complex than a conventional small modular reactor, but said VDL’s experience building such precision equipment gives the company a realistic path to serial production and lower prices.
The asset-light approach is meant to avoid the factory capital a standalone developer would need. Wagner said U.S. competitors might raise $2 billion to build a plant, whereas Emerald Horizon expects its modular approach to avoid a mega-factory, and also to avoid the grid build-out that a large plant would require.
Wagner said the use cases that fit a 10 MW unit include data centers, where a site needing 10 to 20 MW could use a small cluster of containers. Multiple units give built-in redundancy, he said: “If you add six, let’s say, and one would have a problem, the other five are working still.” Other targets include heavy industry, hydrogen production, desalination, and remote or military sites. The company puts the footprint of a complete system at roughly 1,000 square meters, and Müller said the system should run largely under remote control with AI-driven predictive maintenance, though regulators may require staff on site.
The Economics
Wagner said the company is targeting a contract price for SMRX of 8.5 euro cents per kilowatt-hour (¢/kWh) for 20 years under its energy-as-a-service model. He described about 2.2¢ of that as the company’s own cost, paid largely to its manufacturing partner, and about 3.8¢ as profit, with the remaining 2.5¢ a flex margin that the presentation describes as a buffer against cost overruns and room for price negotiation. In the presentation, Emerald Horizon compared that price with 18¢/kWh for German industrial customers including grid fees, levies, and taxes, and 11.5¢/kWh for on-site power without a grid fee. It also calculates that 250 modules at the 3.8¢ margin would produce €790 million in annual profit. The company labels that figure an illustrative calculation based on stated assumptions.
Funding the prototype is a separate matter. The presentation assumes a €75 million prototype cost and up to €150 million more for industrial scale-up. The company reported revenue of about €0.2 million for 2025, which it said in a written response reflects the fact that it has so far been an R&D company. The presentation cites a NuWays AG estimate that group breakeven is not expected before 2029.
Regulation Is the Open Question
Müller said the Netherlands is the best place to start, in part because its government is seeking sites for small modular reactors (SMRs). He said the country is looking for four sites by the end of 2028, and that Haskoning, an engineering consultancy he said employs about 6,000 people, is advising on pre-licensing. He also said the International Atomic Energy Agency expects to release its first SMR guidelines early next year, and that national licensing law will follow.
Emerald Horizon said it plans to build an ADES prototype in Eindhoven, Netherlands, in 2029, together with VDL Groep. Slovakia, where Emerald Horizon has a subsidiary, is a possible location for a demonstration plant, but the company also has “concrete inquiries” from other European countries.
In the U.S., Emerald Horizon has retained Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman LLP to assess whether ADES would fall under a non-reactor, accelerator-and-radiation licensing pathway or a limited advanced-nuclear framework at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. The company has set up a U.S. subsidiary and is seeking U.S. investors. The evening before the interview, Müller said, company officials held a video call with staff at Idaho National Laboratory. Müller said the lab’s message was that “even foreign companies and startups are invited to come over,” though he acknowledged it is “not that easy as for U.S. companies based in the U.S., but there are some options.”
Wagner’s hope is that regulators will classify ADES as “nuclear adjacent” rather than as conventional nuclear. The company’s presentation bases that case on three features: subcritical operation, an external on/off neutron source, and no plutonium or highly enriched uranium added as initial fissile fuel. Whether any regulator will agree is still unknown. “We don’t know it yet,” Wagner said.
— Aaron Larson is POWER’s executive editor.

METiS TechBio’s AiLNP platform uses machine learning models to develop lipid nanoparticles with potentially better tissue specificity that could enhance a drug’s therapeutic performance.
Eli Lilly is tapping Hong Kong–listed METiS TechBio to develop lipid nanoparticle-based drug delivery technology that could allow tissue-specific targeting of certain therapeutic modalities.
Lilly has pledged an upfront commitment “in the low double-digit millions of U.S. dollars,” METiS disclosed in a Monday release . The biotech is also eligible for up to $1.1 billion in development, regulatory and commercial milestones, plus single-digit tiered royalties on net sales of products that arise from the alliance.
The Indianapolis pharma will leverage METiS’ AiLNP platform, which uses AI to discover and optimize ionizable lipids that can be used to produce lipid nanoparticles (LNP) for delivering drugs. The partners didn’t specify which of Lilly’s drugs they plan to package into these lipid spheres or what diseases they want to work on.
BioSpace has reached out to the companies for more details regarding the deal.
LNPs have become a popular method of delivering treatments, especially nucleic acid–based therapies, because they can protect these molecules from destruction and degradation. Several FDA-approved medicines use LNPs, including Alnylam’s RNAi transthyretin amyloidosis therapy Onpattro and Pfizer and BioNTech’s mRNA COVID-19 vaccine Comirnaty .
Through the METiS deal, Lilly is looking to develop novel LNPs “that may enable improved tissue specificity, enhanced therapeutic performance, and broader applicability across multiple disease areas,” according to the Monday announcement.
METiS launched in December 2017 with $86 million in series A capital. Aside from Lilly, the biotech has signed deals with other drugmakers, including China’s Hengrui Pharma in August and Deerfield Management’s Boulevard Bio in June.
The METiS agreement continues what has been a prolific year of dealmaking for Lilly, including up to $870 million pledged earlier this month to expand a partnership with Gate Bioscience to advance therapies against difficult-to-target proteins for conditions with high unmet need.
Other recent Lilly deals include an up to $3.25 billion contract with China’s InnoCare Pharma, covering five targets for undisclosed indications, and the up to $2.88 billion acquisition of Merida Biosciences for a pipeline of autoimmune and allergic disease therapies.

Electrified-Only 2027 Lexus NX SUV Lands with Multiple Upgrades and a Touch of Mars
96 photos
Photo: Lexus
After at the end of last week Japanese luxury carmaker Lexus stepped into the spotlight with the 2027 model year interpretation of the TX SUV, it now does the same for the NX crossover. This time, however, the list of changes imagined for this vehicle is far richer.
Perhaps the most important thing to note about the NX is that from now on there will be no version of it that’s powered exclusively by an internal combustion engine. For 2027, the NX will come to market only as a hybrid and a plug-in hybrid.
The upgrades the carmaker imagined for the refreshed range target, thus, a powertrain realignment, exterior and interior nips and tucks, and a little touch of extra features. Why, for one reason or another, there’s also a connection to planet Mars to discuss.
The overall look of the SUV remains the same as before, but refined in key places in a way that also includes functional elements that target aerodynamics and cooling performance. Finer touches, including a switch from chrome to black for the mirrors and moldings, are also included in the package, as is the first-time use of the double L signature for the rear lamps.
The 2027 NX will be offered on the American market in nine exterior colors, including three new ones: Shaded Ivy, Incognito, and Iridium, which, on top of being a new addition, also replaces the previous Atomic Silver.
Photo: Lexus The cabin of the NX has suffered changes as well, with the most noticeable being the revised steering wheel, which now displays the brand’s name in the new font the company went for this year. On top of that, it’s smaller than it used to be, dropping by 0.4 inches to 14.2 inches.
The dashboard is dominated by the two horizontally aligned screens, the 12.3-inch instrument display and the 14-inch infotainment system. The latter is now offered as standard across all the trim levels.
Lexus throws on the table five interior colors for the NX, two of which, Abalos and Radiant Red, are new. It is here that the connection with planet Mars comes in, as Abalos is, apparently, inspired by the sand dunes that exist in the northern hemisphere of the Red Planet.
As said, there will be only hybrid and plug-in hybrid variants of the NX available for the 2027 model year. When it comes to the former, the chosen name is NX 350h, and the selected powertrain is a combination of a 2.5-liter gasoline engine, a front motor generator, and a rear axle motor. Combined, these bits of hardware are rated at 244 hp, four hp more than in the previous version.
Photo: Lexus The same 2.5-liter gasoline engine is at the core of the plug-in hybrid NX 450h+ as well, only this time it works with a newly developed lithium-ion battery that’s good for up to 45 miles (72 km) of pure electric driving.
The SUV now has an upgraded front electric motor, whose power levels grew from 180 hp to 203 hp, with the one at the rear throwing in an extra 54 hp. The total, combined power of the plug-in hybrid NX stands at 324 hp, 20 more than before.
Technically speaking, the powertrain setup for both versions is not unheard of, but Lexus does speak about having deployed the most advanced hybrid drivetrain technology in the NX, paired with the revised version of the ICE unit.
We’re told about a redesigned engine block casting with reinforced areas for improved block rigidity and reduced noise and vibration. On its own, no matter the application, the engine delivers 186 horsepower at 6,000 rpm and 173 lb-ft of torque at 4,200 rpm.
Photo: Lexus Both versions of the NX are equipped with an e-Axle assembly that brings together in the same package the transaxle, motor, and power control unit. An all-wheel-drive system comes as standard on certain trim levels.
Speaking of configurations, there are three of them for the NX 350h (FWD, AWD, and F Sport), and two for the NX 450h+ (standard and F Sport). The top-of-the-range F Sport brings along, for both powertrains, several unique features, including under spoilers, side pontoons, and rear corner rocker panels, among other things.
These drivetrain setups can be had in combination with no less than six trim levels for the hybrid and four for the plug-in hybrid . For now, Lexus has not released any information on what each of them brings to market.
Lexus did not specifically say when the 2027 NX will become available to order, but it probably won’t be long now. We’ll keep an eye on the Japanese carmaker and report back as soon as it announces how much the refreshed crossover will cost.
Just like before, the new hybrid Lexus NX will be assembled at the Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada (TMMC) facility in Ontario, Canada, while the plug-in hybrid comes from the Toyota Motor Kyushu (TMK) plant in Japan.

Tiny Hot Hatch Just Sold for Porsche Money, Has a Punchy V6 Behind the Seats and a Fatty Widebody
25 photos
Photo: Cars and Bids
This car is not the usual hatchback that gets you from point A to point B with zero excitement. It is, in fact, quite the opposite. The TWR-modified Renault Clio will get you from point A to point B, but you'll want to take the longcut on your way to your destination. It has a V6 behind the front seats, over 200 horsepower, and thrilling road manners.
This 2001 Renault Clio was just sold for $90,000. Scrap everything you know about the standard French hatchback. All those are no longer valid. This car comes with a mid-mounted 3.0-liter V6 petrol engine, which produces 230 horsepower. Not exactly your usual Clio, right?
A manual transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels, which translates to fun behind the wheel, because what you are looking at is one of the most radical factory engineering experiments in automotive history.
Renault took a humble, front-wheel-drive economy commuter tiny car and converted it into the wide-body, mid-engine, rear-wheel-drive monster that you are looking at right now, rubbing your eyes in wonder, unable to understand how someone would pay luxury car money for a tiny hot hatch .
Photo: Cars and Bids The Clio V6 was designed as a sort of spiritual successor to the 1980s Renault 5 Turbo rally legend . Renault unveiled the concept car that previewed it at the 1998 Paris Motor Show as a promotional platform for the Clio V6 Trophy single-make racing series.
But the public went completely wild for it, so the French automaker decided to build a road-going variant. Because Renault's own production lines in Dieppe were busy, they partnered up with Tom Walkinshaw Racing (TWR). The Phase 1 cars were engineered by TWR, had their bodies modified in Finland, and were hand-assembled at TWR’s facility in Uddevalla, Sweden.
To transform a city hatchback into a mid-engine supercar slayer, TWR essentially threw out everything from the front seats backward. The tiny Renault no longer needed anything else. Where the rear bench seat used to be, a structural steel bulkhead was welded.
The 3.0-liter 24-valve V6 engine with naturally aspirated firepower was stuffed sideways into that space. The V6 wasn’t much of an exotic build. It was a modified version of the ES9 V6 used in family haulers such as the Renault Laguna or the Espace minivans.
Photo: Cars and Bids TWR upgraded the power unit with higher-compression pistons, lighter flywheels, and reworked induction ports to bump output to 230 horsepower (233 metric horsepower) and 221 pound-feet (300 Newton meters) of torque.
The engine puts the power down through the rear wheels with the help of the purists’ favorite, a six-speed manual transmission, hooked up to a limited-slip differential. Because the V6 engine had to be mounted transversely, right behind the cockpit where the rear seats used to be, space was incredibly tight.
Renault and Tom Walkinshaw Racing couldn't use a traditional rear-wheel-drive longitudinal gearbox. To achieve a manual transaxle compact enough to sit sideways but strong enough to withstand that amount of torque, Renault adapted the PK6 casing. TWR re-engineered the internals, the linkage setup, and the gear ratios to suit a high-revving sports car.
The new setup did not leave much room for a luggage compartment. The entire trunk was gone. Instead, owners got a tiny 45-liter cargo net behind the front seats and a small 7-liter plastic bucket under the front hood.
Photo: Cars and Bids Because the radiator also sat under the same hood, that space was basically a rolling oven, which meant you could not put groceries there. They would have been cooked by the time you got home.
The car comes with a body kit that makes it absurdly wide, which makes it intimidating next to the stock Clio. It features massive flared wheel arches, gaping side intakes to feed and cool the mid-mounted engine, and rides on 17-inch OZ racing wheels.
Surprisingly, while the exterior looked like that of a track-ready car, the interior was largely standard, sporting the then-cheap Clio layout, in which bucket seats upholstered in Alcantara were installed. A number plaque on the center console confirmed that the car was actually something special.
How special? 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 6.0 seconds special. A top speed of 146 mph (235 kph) special. With the very short wheelbase, a lightweight construction, and a rigid suspension out back, the driver has to know his way around the rear-wheel-drive pocket rocket to prevent uncontrollable tail dancing .
Photo: Cars and Bids Only 1,513 such cars saw the light of day between 2001 and 2003, and the one that just sold for $90,000 is one of them. Because these cars were never legally imported brand-new in the United States, they are the highly coveted forbidden fruit for American collectors.
However, now that early 2001 models cross the 25-year threshold required for legal U.S. import, pristine, low-mileage survivors like this 30,281-kilometer (18,815-mile) example have skyrocketed into genuine collector status.
Finished in Iceberg Silver with a blue and gray interior, the Renault-badged missile has just been handed over to its new owner with one key, Japanese-language service records, and a couple of flaws like scratches on the front plastic lip spoiler and bumper, along with signs of wear on the center console trim and shifter boot.
However, those flaws did not scare the buyer off. he paid Porsche Cayenne money for a tiny Renault that won’t win him races at the track, but will surely shock other motorists when flashing from stoplight to stoplight.

By Alison Koo
20 October 2026
Singapore’s position as a global container transhipment hub depends on its ability to remain competitive within international liner shipping networks, as rival ports accelerate investment in digitalisation and automation.
At the Singapore Port Workers Union’s 80th anniversary dinner on Sunday, senior minister Lee Hsien Loong (pictured) said Singapore’s port competitiveness could not be taken for granted, and warned that complacency at PSA International risked losing business to competing ports.
Unlike major Chinese gateways such as Shanghai and Ningbo-Zhoushan, which benefit from substantial domestic volumes, Singapore relies heavily on transhipment traffic and its role as a connecting hub for global shipping lines. Maintaining this position required the port to continually improve efficiency, productivity, and operational capabilities to remain attractive to carriers, he said.
Mr Lee, who was Singapore’s prime minister from 2004 to 2024, cited Shanghai’s Yangshan port as an example of a competitor making significant advances in automation and digitalisation. As rival ports upgrade their infrastructure and operations, Singapore would need to continue investing to preserve its competitive edge and retain shipping customers.
The challenge is particularly important as Singapore consolidates container operations from Tanjong Pagar, Brani, Keppel ,and Pasir Panjang at Tuas. The new port is expected to have an annual handling capacity of 65m teu by the 2040s, with technology playing a central role in increasing throughput and maximising productivity, amid the country’s land constraints.
Singapore handled almost 45m teu in 2025, while throughput in the first half of this year was up 4.7% year on year, to 22.7m teu.
Mr Lee’s warning reflected Singapore’s experience in the 2000s, when it lost Taiwan’s Evergreen to Malaysia’s new Tanjung Pelepas port, prompting PSA to cut jobs in 2003, and restructure operations to restore competitiveness. Although Evergreen returned to Singapore in 2024 after securing a terminal concession with PSA, the episode illustrates the risks of losing business in an industry where shipping lines can redirect their networks towards competing hubs.
Mr Lee said: “Apart from competition from other ports, the industry itself is transforming in fundamental ways. Supply chain disruptions, climate change, geopolitical tensions are all affecting shippers and port operators. Rapid advances in AI, autonomous technology, sensors, and robotics are already dramatically transforming port operations.”
For Singapore, maintaining its position would, therefore, depend on more than expanding capacity at Tuas: it would require sustained technological advancement and continuous adaptation to the changing demands of global liner shipping networks, he said.
Mr Lee added: “These developments present new challenges, but also new opportunities. There’ll be higher-value tasks which are less physically demanding; better jobs, centred on data, judgment, and decision making. PSA must keep abreast of these changes and reinvent itself…..to turn these new challenges into opportunities.”

By Charlotte Goldstone
20 October 2026
WiseTech Global has integrated its CargoWise Landside transport management systems (TMS) with marine terminal appointment software provider Dray Dog, enabling US drayage operators to automate port bookings and reduce manual data entry.
The integration connects Dray Dog with CargoWise’s Trinium, Profit Tools, and Compcare management systems, allowing dispatchers and customer service representatives to receive confirmed appointment details, including reference numbers, directly within their own TMS.
Dray Dog, a CargoSprint company, automates the process of securing marine terminal appointments by continuously retrieving available slots, and booking them according to predefined carrier parameters.
Container and operational data is exchanged between the systems, with information sent from the TMS to initiate scheduling and confirmed bookings returned, to update loads and dispatch plans in real time, and appointment details can also flow to driver-facing applications.
The move targets a longstanding administrative burden for drayage operators at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach that must coordinate terminal availability, appointment bookings, dispatch systems, and driver schedules across multiple platforms.
Former Harbour Trucking Association CEO Matt Schrap previously told The Loadstar : “You’re operating across several different platforms, not only in the port ecosystem, but within your own company. You deal with availability from the carrier or terminal, then find an appointment, then interface with dispatch software, just to get a truck out of the gate.
“To have a person doing that doesn’t make sense when software exists. It’s about efficiency.”
According to Mark Rabens, SVP transportation at Custom Goods & Quik Pick Express, the Trinium TMS-Dray Dog integration will ultimately save time and money, while improving customer service levels. He added that the ability to book earlier appointments would reduce “supply chain lag”.
And Jon Steitzer, head of Dray Dog, added: “Every minute counts in drayage.
“We built Dray Dog to give truckers the best possible tool to manage appointments at every step of the container lifecycle. Connecting with CargoWise Landside is exactly the kind of partnership that solves real problems, and delivers on our mission of helping drayage truckers win.”
Dennis Lane, head of revenue for CargoWise Landside Solutions, added: “By automating one of their most repetitive and time-sensitive tasks, the Dray Dog integration delivers immediate productivity gains.”

Renault Issues Fire Risk Recall for Captur and Symbioz Hybrid Vehicles
8 photos
Photo: Renault
A small number of Captur and Symbioz crossovers are being recalled in Europe because of a potentially compromised busbar-to-relay connection inside the traction battery. A bad joint in the high-voltage battery of a hybrid vehicle is not the kind of thing you or even Renault ignore.
Per the European Commission's Safety Gate rapid alert system for dangerous non-food products, the recall covers Captur and Symbioz hybrids produced between December 1, 2025, and February 6, 2026. The French automaker uses 0FDZ to identify said campaign.
The vehicles in question are based on the CMF-B platform, with both the Captur and Symbioz hailing from the Valladolid plant in Spain. Although they are identical in many respects, the Captur is a bit shorter than its brother. Featuring an extended overhang, the wagon-like Symbioz offers a bit more luggage space while retaining the Captur's wheelbase.
Regarding the problem per se, the busbar is the conductive bar that carries current within the battery. A relay creates resistance at the joint, and resistance turns current into heat. Too much of it, and the lithium-ion battery could very well sign off in a ball of fire.
The Safety Gate description of the problem reads that abnormal heating of the connection and battery cells may result in a fire, but no such fires have been reported thus far in the European space. Renault 's local subsidiaries will send owners registered letters asking them to book a service appointment.
Photo: Renault The fix should take no more than four hours and 30 minutes, traction battery inspection included. Renault is most certainly offering courtesy vehicles during the downtime period. As of this writing, the Symbioz hybrid is sold in France as the E-Tech 160 with 158 mechanical ponies to its name. It's joined by a lower-output gasoline and bi-fuel version with 120 chevaux-vapeur.
Instead of 29,990 euros for the Eco-G with the manual box, the full-hybrid model retails at 34,400 euros. The Captur sits below it, with prices kicking off at 26,800 euros for the Eco-G and 27,300 euros for the TCe. Upgrading to the noticeably more frugal hybrid means 30,500 euros from the outset.
Competing against the Peugeot 2008, Toyota Yaris Cross, and the Volkswagen T-Roc, the Captur is one of the best-selling crossovers in France. It and the Symbioz maintain consistent placement in the country's top 20 best sellers, with Renault being the leading automotive brand in France.
The group as a whole experienced a successful year in 2025, driven by strong demand for electrified vehicles in the core brand's home market. Renault alone sold more than a million vehicles across the continent, ranking second overall, while French registrations totaled nearly 285,600 vehicles in 2025. When it comes to best-selling passenger vehicle overall in France, the Renault Clio made easy work of second-placed Peugeot 208 and third-placed Dacia Sandero.

One of the quieter but more consequential points to come out of a recent candid session with Daimler Truck leadership had nothing to do with financing or freight rates and everything to do with how the trucks themselves are being built right now, because the company made clear that it is already producing a Freightliner Cascadia engineered to be autonomy-ready straight off the assembly line, with the hardware for driverless operation designed in from the factory rather than bolted on later as an afterthought.
For any fleet thinking about where its next generation of equipment fits into a future that includes self-driving trucks, this detail matters more than the headline timelines, because it speaks to whether the truck you buy is a dead end or a platform. Here is what Daimler’s leadership described about building autonomy into the chassis, why the company is deliberately keeping the software choice open, and what that means for fleet decision-makers weighing long-term equipment strategy.
Redundancy Built In At The Factory
The foundation of an autonomous truck is not the self-driving software, it is the hardware underneath it that can be trusted to respond when no human hand is on the wheel. A truck driven by a computer needs systems that do not have a single point of failure, because there is no driver to take over if something quits.
Daimler’s answer is what it calls an autonomy-ready Cascadia built on a redundant chassis, with full redundancy in braking and steering. In plain terms, the critical control systems that stop and steer the truck are doubled up, engineered so that if one path fails, a backup is already in place to keep the vehicle safe. Eva Scherer, chief financial officer of Daimler Truck Holding AG, pointed to this redundant platform as a core reason the company believes it is uniquely positioned in North America, where it is the market leader. That redundancy is the assembly-line preparation that makes everything else possible, because it turns a conventional truck into a base that a virtual driver can eventually operate.
The significance for a fleet is that this is not a retrofit story. The truck is being manufactured with the autonomous foundation already present, which changes how a buyer should think about the equipment coming off the line today and in the near future. It is being designed as a platform that can grow into autonomy rather than a vehicle that would need to be torn apart and rebuilt to get there.
The Software Choice Is Deliberately Left Open
The more strategically interesting decision is what Daimler is doing on top of that redundant chassis, and it is a choice that directly affects fleet risk. Rather than hard-wiring the truck to a single self-driving company, the company is building the platform to remain adaptable.
Scherer explained that while Daimler is currently working with the redundant Cascadia and the virtual driver from its subsidiary Torc Robotics, the redundant chassis is set up so that it can ultimately run with various autonomous companies’ virtual drivers. The offering is being designed as modular, and explicitly not exclusive to a single provider. On top of the redundant chassis, an AV kit, the sensor and computing hardware that the self-driving system needs, gets fitted to the cab, and the specifications of that kit vary depending on which virtual-driver company’s technology is going in. So the truck provides a common, autonomy-ready foundation, and the specific self-driving system becomes a modular layer installed according to each provider’s requirements.
This matters because the autonomous-trucking landscape is still shaking out, and the companies developing virtual drivers are in a race whose winners are not yet settled. A fleet that locks its equipment to one self-driving vendor is making a bet on that vendor surviving and leading. By keeping the chassis provider-agnostic, Daimler is preserving optionality, both for itself and for the customer, so that the hardware investment is not stranded if the software landscape shifts. For a fleet leader, that is the difference between buying a truck tied to one company’s fate and buying a platform that can adapt as the technology and the market evolve.
Where This Fits In The Timeline
The factory-level readiness is not an abstraction waiting on some distant future. Daimler’s leadership laid out a concrete near-term path. The company said it expects to get the driver out on a first route by the end of this year, then build up the mileage it is running, and move toward commercialization at scale around 2028. The rollout will come on defined lanes that expand gradually, with safety treated as the gating factor at every step.
Scherer also described how quickly the underlying capability is advancing, noting a shift from older imitation-based training methods to reinforcement learning, which allows a truck to handle routes it has never seen before. That is a meaningful change, because it moves autonomy from something that has to be painstakingly mapped lane by lane toward a system that can expand geographically faster. Her read was that the next couple of years will bring a quick expansion, which puts the autonomy-ready trucks rolling off the line now squarely on the runway toward real commercial use rather than years of waiting.
The Business Model That Rides On Top
The way the truck is built also shapes how it will eventually be paid for, and the two are connected. Because the autonomous capability is a modular layer added on top of the truck rather than baked into a single inseparable product, Daimler is structuring the business around separate revenue streams. A fleet buys or finances the truck and the chassis the way it always has, and the virtual driver comes as a per-mile software-as-a-service charge layered on top.
That separation is a direct consequence of the design philosophy. A provider-agnostic, modular chassis naturally lends itself to a model where the metal and the driving capability are priced as distinct things, the truck as a capital asset and the autonomous system as an ongoing subscription tied to the miles it actually drives. Daimler said it is still refining that business model but is prepared to finance whatever shape it ultimately takes, customizing its approach around how the market develops. For a fleet, the takeaway is that the hardware decision and the eventual software-and-service decision can be made somewhat independently, which again preserves flexibility rather than forcing an all-in commitment up front.
Why It Matters
Building the autonomy-ready chassis at the factory and keeping it open to multiple self-driving providers is a strategic choice that turns the truck from a fixed product into a platform, and it directly reduces the risk a fleet takes on when it buys equipment heading into an uncertain autonomous future. For fleet and finance leaders, the practical significance is optionality, because a provider-agnostic, redundant platform means a hardware investment made today is less likely to be stranded by a shakeout among virtual-driver companies, and the capability can be added as a modular, per-mile layer when the lanes and the economics are right rather than demanded as an expensive bet up front.
