Three Failed Brake Pedal Brackets Put Chinese Luxury Minivan Under Investigation
22 photos
Photo: Dongchedi
Three units of the Maextro V800 went through emergency stop testing at the beginning of October 2026. All three Chinese luxury minivans suffered brake pedal bracket failures, which is unacceptable in this day and age, regardless of vehicle segment and body style. For a luxury MPV that launched barely two months earlier, that is a very serious problem.
China 's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology opened an investigation on October 15, 2026, and this investigation could be a lot more interesting than Maextro's rebuttal of the failed tests. It all started on October 8 with Dongchedi, namely the ByteDance-controlled automotive platform that is also known as DCar.
The video published that day saw Dongchedi perform emergency braking tests from 100 kilometers per hour (62 miles per hour) to a standstill on a closed course. The first Maextro V800's brake pedal bracket failed on its third attempt, the second on its fourth, and a subsequently purchased Maextro V800 gave up the ghost on attempt two.
Needless to say, there's a distinction to make between a failed bracket and a wholesale braking system defect. According to Dongchedi, the fractures prevented normal brake pedal operation. The emergency braking function did activate, though, providing deceleration after the brake pedal bracket had failed.
Due to said problem, stopping distances increased from around 38 meters (125 feet) on average to approximately 140 meters (459 feet) when the emergency braking function took over. Dongchedi gave a few suggestions about bracket geometry, reinforcement, and material, but all of these details have yet to be professionally investigated by actual safety boffins and Maextro engineers.
Photo: Dongchedi Speaking of, Maextro answered on the evening of October 8, 2026. Describing itself as an ultra-luxury electric vehicle brand, the brand in question should be viewed as a joint venture between the JAC Group and Huawei. Per the automaker's representatives, no bracket fractures had been reported by V800 customers since deliveries began. Maextro also maintained that development and validation exceeded industry requirements.
The fun part? Maextro said the Dongchedi video shows nonstandard extreme conditions. Truth be told, nonstandard extreme braking conditions can also occur during daily driving scenarios. While Maextro stopped short of describing the Dongchedi test as invalid, the absence of customer failure reports does not explain the three Dongchedi failures. Whataboutism, if you will.
Worse still for Maextro , the company also promised engineering changes before the MIIT started looking into this matter on October 15, 2026. The automaker's October 8 response pledged an improved bracket base design, a free upgrade for existing Maextro V800 owners, improved testing parameters, and changes to production quality management.
A promised free upgrade is not the same as a recall, though, and that is probably the reason why the MIIT started an investigation of its own. Be that as it may, the October 15 notice is much narrower than the argument around it. The MIIT investigates the alleged defect with the help of the Cyberspace Administration and the State Administration for Market Regulation.

Big-Finned Farm Find: 1960 Plymouth Fury Runs and Drives After 28 Years
14 photos
Photo: Street Rat Garage/YouTube
When it comes to styling features we no longer get on cars, I'm particularly nostalgic about the tail fins. These emerged in the late 1940s and became rather huge toward the end of the next decade. Most American carmakers dropped the fins in the early 1960s .
The 1959 Cadillacs had the largest and most extravagant tail fins, but I'm a fan of the 1957-1960 Mopars. That's because I'm also a sucker for Virgil Exner's "Forward Look" design language, which works best with big fins in my book. My favorite model years? Well, I'm finding it difficult to pick one, but 1960 is among the top three.
And this brings me to the 1960 Plymouth Fury you see here. Although it's often overshadowed by the 1957-1959 iterations, I think that the 1960 Fury is by far the more flamboyant iteration. I like the heavily sculpted front fenders, the lowered headlamps, and the slightly smaller grille. The rear end with the larger fins and the vertical taillights is also a great improvement over the 1959 version.
The 1960 Fury was a massive redesign compared to its predecessor. It's the first year of the second-gen Fury, replacing the first-generation model after only one year. Although the Fury debuted in 1956, it did not become a stand-alone model until 1959 (it was a sub-series of the Belvedere).
The 1960 Fury is also a one-year-only design. The 1961 version is also considered a second-gen model, but Plymouth made radical changes design-wise. Not only did it drop the fins, but it also revised the front fascia, which gained horizontal fin-like elements above the headlamps. A face that only a mother could love, according to many.
The 1960 Fury was pretty popular, moving about 63,000 units. Despite this, it's a rare sight on public roads today. Many of these cars were parked and never maintained, while others were dumped into junkyards when their owners upgraded to more modern vehicles. This four-door sedan is one of those cars. It was parked in a field in the 1990s and hasn't been moved since.
Rescued by YouTube's "Street Rat Garage," the Fury was last registered in 1998. This means that it's been sitting without a sip of gasoline for nearly 30 years as of 2026. That's a very long time, especially if the car was parked outside, under full exposure to the elements. But despite all that, the Fury is still in decent shape.
While most farm finds display severe rust issues, this Mopar is still clean. Sure, the paint is weathered and the tires are far too gone, but there's next to no rust to talk about. It's still very much complete apart from the missing steering wheel and door panel.
But it does have a few notable issues. The original headliner is gone, replaced by a strange fabric with a wooden element in the center. The front bench seat was also reupholstered, but someone did a terrible job. The white/red combo, which is different from the original two-tone tan seen in the rest of the cabin, suggests that the upholstery was sourced from a different car.
As for the engine, there's good news and bad news. The good news is that the Fury still relies on its factory powerplant. The bad news is that it doesn't have a V8. Although the Fury was originally a performance-oriented model, it gained an inline-six as standard equipment in 1960.
This Fury packs the entry-level 225-cubic-inch (3.7-liter) Slant-Six, which was marketed as the "economy six" at the time. The one-barrel produced 145 horsepower, a rather low figure for a full-size car tipping the scales at over 3,500 pounds (1,588 kg).
But hey, I'm not going to complain here. These cars rarely get saved, so I'm excited to see it in someone's garage. Moreover, the new owner also got the engine running, and it seems that the Fury still has what it takes to drive under its own power (although it still needs brakes). This Mopar deserves to become road-worthy again.

Tesla Sets December 3 Shareholder Meeting Amid Rumors of an Imminent SpaceX Merger
8 photos
Photo: Tesla
Tesla announced a shareholder meeting on December 3, two weeks after the third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday. Tesla shareholders are asked to vote on re-electing three directors, including Elon Musk, approving the 2025 executive compensation package, and naming PwC as Tesla's auditor for 2026. There's no official word about an anticipated Tesla-SpaceX merger.
October was hailed as one of the most consequential months of 2026 for Tesla and Elon Musk's other companies. The carmaker has unveiled a second variant of the Roadster that can fly, roll, and land, a PR stunt seen as a warm-up for a possible SpaceX-Tesla merger. Both companies are holding their third-quarter earnings calls this week, with SpaceX on Tuesday and Tesla on Wednesday. For SpaceX, this also comes after a successful Starship launch on September 28.
Unsurprisingly, Elon Musk is looking to bank on these successes with an anticipated announcement of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Days before the third-quarter earnings call, Tesla called the annual shareholder meeting on December 3. The official agenda doesn't mention the merger, but that is still looming large and will likely be discussed during the meeting.
Officially, the shareholder meeting has three proposals on the ballot, and none is about the merger. Tesla wants its shareholders to re-elect Elon Musk, Robyn Denholm, and JB Straubel to Tesla's Board of Directors and to approve PwC as Tesla's auditor for 2026. Shareholders are also asked to vote on 2025 executive compensation, including about $158.4 billion in 2025 stock awards to Musk.
Elon Musk hasn't ruled out a merger between SpaceX and Tesla , but has said in the past that an earnings call was not the place to discuss it. This would be the role of a shareholder meeting. If we don't see the merger talks mentioned in the proxy statement, it's because Tesla can't hold a vote until it fulfills certain requirements, which include informing the shareholders about this intention.
The proxy statement does include some hints at such a move, if that was not clear enough already. For instance, the statement confirms that Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs both Tesla's compensation committee and its governance committee, is also a member of the SpaceX board since February. Another sign is even clearer to pave the way for a future merger: automatic voting.
Specifically, the meeting marks the debut of Tesla's Voluntary Retail Voting Program, which essentially locks investor votes with the board for future votes. There are two options, with one being to vote your shares with the board on everything, while the second leaves out so-called "special matters," including director elections or mergers that need shareholder approval. There's no option to auto-vote against the board.
This means that shareholders who pick "All Matters" when opting for the program will have their shares automatically counted for the board's position on a merger. This should make it easier to pass a vote and avoid an embarrassment like the one cast in November 2025. Back then, the Tesla board attempted to eliminate the supermajority voting requirements, but couldn't get enough shares to pass the bar. While the auto-vote mandate does not apply to the December 3 vote, it will count in the next shareholder meeting.
There are several indications that Tesla and SpaceX are preparing to announce a merger. Musk has been trying for a long time to tie the two companies in joint projects, and last week's Roadster PR stunt is but an example. Immediately following the event, SpaceX executives have started following Tesla social media accounts and vice versa, supposedly for more than just seeing their Halloween posts.
Analysts expect the SpaceX earnings call tonight and Tesla's tomorrow to provide a clearer picture of what a Tesla-SpaceX merger will look like. The most likely scenario is an all-stock deal, with SpaceX buying Tesla at a premium. This means that Tesla shares will convert into SpaceX stock, and the third-quarter results will effectively set the price for this conversion. Last year, we laid out our vision for building a world of amazing abundance – this year, it’s been coming to life. And we’re only getting started… Your vote is critical to helping us maintain that momentum. Voting instructions & control numbers to follow soon. Subaru's In-House Electric Vehicle Outputs 510 HP, Uses Aisin Drive Units, Panasonic Battery Cells

Subaru has recently stuffed a 380-kilowatt electric drive system under a heavily modified Outback body shell. Underpinned by a completely new platform, this mule previews a future model that should give Scooby more control over its electric vehicles than the current Toyota-shared family allows.
As reported by Automotive News, the zero-emission mule is good for approximately 510 horsepower and under four seconds to 100 kilometers per hour (62 miles per hour). Its wheelbase exceeds that of the donor vehicle, forcing a few interesting cuts around the wheel openings. That sort of awkwardness is customary of mules rather than pre-production prototypes.
The front motor apparently makes 150 kilowatts (201 horsepower) at full chatter, while its rear-mounted brother supplies 230 kilowatts (308 horsepower) in optimal conditions. More power and torque at the back gives the EV-centric platform a different starting point from a symmetrical pair of drive units, establishing a rear-biased setup. The control strategy, however, is a mystery for the time being.
As per engineering executive Takatomo Watamori, the Aisin-supplied motors were not selected for grunt alone. Instead, the Japanese automaker wants to preserve Subaru's trademark all-wheel-drive and safety priorities. Going independent with the development of this platform does not mean locking suppliers out, as demonstrated by the Aisin drive units.
Aisin, which is part of Toyota's larger group, remains the e-axle partner. Subaru announced this collab in March 2024, describing joint development and shared production of compact drive units. Panasonic, meanwhile, supplies battery expertise. Said relationships give Subaru architectural ownership, which is precisely the point of this project.
Photo: Subaru Its partnership with Toyota has already produced four models, namely the Solterra, Uncharted, Trailseeker, and Getaway. From the looks of it, the mule appears to fall somewhere between the dimensions of the Trailseeker and Getaway. The crash structure of the newcomer features new support members that curve over the front wheels to guide impact loads.
The front motor can rotate during a collision, thus absorbing energy. Subaru engineers aim to protect both occupants and the underfloor battery in the event of a crash. The company also targets a weight reduction of 100 kilograms (220 pounds) compared to the e-TNGA of Toyota, which is a modular design that also underpins the Lexus RZ and the Toyota C-HR+.
A lighter structure and better crash protection make for a great combination, and Subaru also worked its magic with the mule's battery pack. It contains nearly 4,000 cylindrical Panasonic cells, with the pack weighing 25 percent less than its e-TNGA batteries while targeting an energy density 20 percent above the industry average. Panasonic's involvement also dates back to March 2024.
Automotive News further learned about an integrated control unit covering powertrain, chassis, infotainment, and driver assistance duties, using a customized AMD SoC that supports over-the-air updates. Subaru wants to manufacture the units itself and share them across the lineup.
The final piece of the puzzle is Subaru confirming work with Infineon in March 2026 on a microcontroller for the integrated ECU, and this work is also expected to include AI integration into the EyeSight driver-assistance suite.

Certain 2026 Ram 2500 Trucks Could Lose Stability Control Without Warning
32 photos
Photo: Ram
Towing 20,000 pounds, which is 9,072 kilos in metric speak, in a properly equipped 2026 Ram 2500 is asking a lot of the cooling system, driveline, and brakes. You are further asking a lot of the ESC, specifically the system that decides which wheel to brake and how much torque to cut when the back end starts to dance.
FCA US LLC has recalled 8,329 of these pickups because a steering column module can switch electronic stability control off without giving the driver any warning. Referred to as 26V651 in NHTSA vernacular, the campaign covers 2026 models exclusively. Affected trucks were produced between September 13, 2025, and November 15, 2025, for the United States market.
The subject module lives in the steering column and handles a bunch of driver inputs and related signals. If the SCCM develops an internal fault, said module can disable electronic stability control, thus increasing the risk of a crash at high speeds. Per Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 126, electronic stability control must stay active while driving.
As for the part that should bother affected owners, the ESC light only comes on after the module resets. A three-quarter-ton pickup is not the kind of vehicle where you want to experience that while towing on the highway. The 2026 model offers a 6.4-liter HEMI naturally aspirated V8 with quite a bit of torque under its belt, or an optional 6.7-liter Cummins turbo diesel I6 with quite a bit more torque.
The advertised maximum towing capacity of 20,000 pounds is for properly equipped Cummins trucks. Electronic stability control uses targeted braking and engine torque management to keep the vehicle on the driver's intended line. Losing ESC when intervention is relied upon is the perfect recipe for disaster.
Photo: Ram Stellantis North America started investigating the recall condition back in July 2026. Field records and customer assistance records were reviewed through September 2026, helping the Technical Safety and Regulatory Compliance group recognize the noncompliance condition. By the end of September 2026, the Vehicle Regulations Committee had heard enough.
Rather than a reflash of the module, the remedy comes in the guise of a replacement module. A newly designed steering column module will be fitted at no charge to affected customers. Ram dealers nationwide have already been notified, while customer notifications are due on November 24, 2026, at the earliest. VINs for suspect trucks are now searchable on the NHTSA's website.
Competing against Ford 's F-250, the Chevrolet division's Silverado 2500, and the mechanically similar GMC Sierra 2500, the Ram 2500 carries a starting price of $46,855 for model year 2026. Its base specification is the Tradesman grade with rear-wheel drive, the regular cab, eight-foot box, and the HEMI engine.
For 2027, the starting price is $48,040 before destination charge. Beyond the work-oriented trim, prospective customers are further presented with the Big Horn, Black Express, and Laramie trims. Those prepared to spend in excess of $70,000 on a 2500 are presented with the Rebel, Power Wagon, Limited, and Longhorn. The latter starts at $75,505 sans the $2,795 freight charge.

Rapport Therapeutics clocked its second Phase 2 win in 14 months for RAP-219—which the company is positioning as a potential pipeline-in-a-product—this time showing improvement in symptoms of bipolar mania.
Shares of Rapport Therapeutics spiked early Tuesday morning after the biotech’s lead candidate showed significant improvement in bipolar mania symptoms in a mid-stage trial.
The Phase 2 trial , which was studying RAP-219 in 253 adults with acute bipolar mania, “just hits,” with acceptable safety, Stifel analysts wrote in a note to investors Tuesday morning.
Indeed, the trial met its primary endpoint as treatment with RAP-219 led to a 3.1-point placebo-adjusted improvement at three weeks on a scale measuring symptoms of the illness, the biotech reported on Tuesday. The Young Mania Rating Scale—the most commonly used rating scale in mania research, according to Rapport—measures 11 core symptoms, including elevated mood, increased activity and energy.
Patients taking Rapport’s drug saw a 15.4-point reduction in symptoms while placebo comparators had a reduction of 12.3 points.
Stifel called the trial win a “clear positive” against a backdrop of low expectations, however noting that the 3.1pt effect-size “just met statistical significance (p=0.045) and was on the lower-end of the range that’s considered competitive with available drugs today (3-4pts).”
RAP-219 also succeeded on the pre-specified secondary endpoint, showing a statistically significant improvement in mania severity score versus placebo at week three on a scale reflecting a clinician’s overall judgment of symptom severity.

Equally important, Stifel said, is that “safety here actually looks pretty good.”
RAP-219 was well-tolerated, Rapport said, with no severe treatment emergent adverse events (TEAEs) or serious adverse events (SAEs) observed over the treatment period.
“For people with bipolar disorder, the challenge isn’t just finding a treatment that’s efficacious. It’s finding one they can tolerate and stay on,” Rapport CEO Abraham Ceesay said in a prepared statement. “Side effects drive discontinuation, and discontinuation drives relapse. RAP-219 has the potential to break that cycle with the first new mechanism of action for bipolar mania in decades.”
Shares of the biotech shot up more than 25% to $35.88 in premarket trading on Tuesday—though they stabilized upon market open, with the stock trading down about 2%.
Rapport declared in its press release that the result is clinical proof-of-concept for RAP-219’s novel TARPγ8-selective mechanism in bipolar mania, adding that the data support moving the program into Phase 3 trials, which are expected to begin in the second half of 2027.
RAP-219 is a TARPγ8-specific AMPA receptor (AMPAR) negative allosteric modulator. Neuro-imaging studies in patients with bipolar disorder show that the hippocampus, a region of the brain in which TARPγ8 is expressed, exhibits abnormal activation and hyperactivity, according to Rapport’s website . On the other hand, TARPγ8 is minimally expressed in the hindbrain, where drug effects are often associated with intolerable adverse events, Rapport noted in its announcement. This gives RAP-219 the potential to provide “a differentiated profile as compared to traditional neuroscience medications.”
The positive topline readout for RAP-219 in bipolar mania continues a positive run for the asset. In September 2025, Phase 2a data in drug-resistant focal epilepsy exceeded analyst and Wall Street expectations, reducing seizures by almost 78%. Rapport shares jumped more than 180% on the news. A federal trials database lists two Phase 3 trials in this indication, one that kicked off last month and another in June.
“Rapport now has clinical proof-of-concept in an indication beyond epilepsy, which builds on RAP-219’s multi-blockbuster potential heading into a Phase 3 program in second half 2027,” William Blair analysts wrote on Tuesday.
Ceesay added in his statement that the two datasets show the asset “delivering on its potential as a pipeline-in-a-product with two indications that both represent multibillion dollar market opportunities.”

The cargo division of Qantas Airways has taken delivery of the first of three additional Airbus A321 converted freighters it will operate for Australia Post to help meet growing demand for expedited parcel delivery across Australia.
The arrival of the new aircraft just weeks before Black Friday sales and the peak Christmas shipping season will help Australia Post and Qantas Freight keep up with increased demand from millions of online shoppers in Australia for overnight and next-day delivery.
The additional two A321 cargo jets are scheduled to join the Qantas fleet by March.
Together, the three aircraft will add up to 20% capacity to the Qantas operated dedicated freighter network, increasing the capability to carry up to 20,000 Australia Post and StarTrack parcels on each flight, the companies said in a joint news release Monday.
StarTrack is a wholly owned subsidiary of Australia Post that provides courier services.
Qantas Freight has eight A321 cargo jets, six of which are dedicated to support Australia Post. The new additions will give Australia Post nine dedicated A321s, all of which are used passenger jets that have been reconfigured by Elbe Flugzeugwerke, a joint venture between Airbus and Singapore’s ST Engineering, to carry containers on the main deck.
Under a 10-year contract extension last summer , Qantas Freight will also operate two Airbus A330 medium widebody freighters for Australia Post, and reserve space on Qantas passenger aircraft to carry shipments on behalf of the national postal operator.
The newest A321 freighter will be based at Qantas Freight’s new terminal at Western Sydney International Airport, which opened for business in July.
“These new aircraft will help us move more parcels across our network and provide additional capacity at a time when online shopping continues to grow and major retail events are driving record parcel volumes,” said Mark Davis, Australia Post’s general manager for linehaul fleet and special services, in the announcement. “Together with Qantas, we’re investing in the infrastructure that keeps Australia connected. The addition of these aircraft, alongside the opening of Western Sydney International Airport’s 24-hour freight terminal, will help strengthen the resilience and capacity of our network for years to come.”
Why It Matters: Australia Post and Qantas represent one of the few positive case studies for the A321 converted freighter since it entered the market six years ago. The promise of the aircraft as a replacement for the aging Boeing 757 converted freighter has not materialized. Conversion orders have been lower than expected and some airlines, including Lufthansa Cargo, have given up on the aircraft . Industry consensus is that the A321 works well in high frequency e-commerce routes where the plane’s volume is well suited for lightweight packages, but that the Boeing 737-800 converted freighter is better for general cargo.

Credit: Polestar
Polestar and the University of Oxford put 12 drivers in eye trackers and heart-rate monitors and sent them around a Swedish racetrack in two versions of the Polestar 4. The goal was to put numbers on something no spec sheet captures: how performance feels to the person driving.
The 544 hp Polestar 4 Dual motor with Performance pack delivered 32% higher peak acceleration than the 268 hp Rear motor version on matched laps, and it needed 15% less steering effort to do it. Drivers also rated it far higher on the experience.
How Oxford and Polestar tried to measure the “feel” of performance
The pilot study comes from researchers at the University of Oxford’s SDG Impact Lab, working with Polestar. It took place at the Gotland Ring, a track built inside an old limestone quarry on the Swedish island of Gotland.
Credit: Polestar
Each participant drove both cars in calm and dynamic conditions:
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Polestar 4 Rear motor: 200 kW (268 hp)
Polestar 4 Dual motor with Performance pack: 400 kW (544 hp)
The researchers logged vehicle telemetry alongside heart-rate data, eye tracking and psychological assessments, then interviewed the drivers afterward. The idea is to line up what the car was doing at a given moment with what was happening to the human inside it.
Credit: Polestar
Photos from the test also show drivers wearing electrode caps, though brain activity isn’t among the measures Polestar published results for.
Several of those measures reacted when the driving got more intense. In dynamic driving, participants blinked less, their pupils got bigger, and they held their gaze longer on a given point. Researchers read that as deeper attention. They could also tie moments in the telemetry to changes in the drivers’ physiological activation.
32% more acceleration, 15% less steering effort
The car-to-car comparison is the most concrete part of the study. On matched fast laps, where both versions were driven at virtually the same pace, the Performance pack car hit 32% higher peak acceleration while requiring 15% less steering effort. It also pulled bigger cornering loads and logged more hard-acceleration events.
That steering figure is the one I’d focus on. You’d expect twice the power to mean more work for the driver at the same lap time. Instead, the dual-motor car asked less of them.
Credit: Polestar
The drivers’ own scores moved in the same direction. On the study’s Performance/Dynamics scale, the Performance version scored 89.2 out of 100, versus 67.7 for the Rear motor. Overall experiential quality came in at 93.0 versus 77.9, with most drivers rating the Performance version higher on both.
“A controlled roller coaster”
The interviews are where it gets more human. Drivers didn’t describe performance as pure adrenaline. They talked about a mix of physical arousal, trust in the car, a sense of control, and intense focus. Several of them, independently, landed on the same image: a “controlled roller coaster.”
One participant said the car “makes you feel like a better driver than you are.” Researchers found drivers linked that combination of thrill, trust and control more consistently to the Performance version.
Max Klapow, a doctoral researcher at the Oxford SDG Impact Lab, framed it this way:
“Performance is not simply about going faster. It is about giving the driver a sense of confidence and control through predictable vehicle responses.”
Christian Samson, Polestar’s head of product attributes, said the company wanted to understand “something that can’t be captured by a specification sheet alone.”
Now, the caveats. The researchers themselves call this a feasibility pilot and say a larger study is needed to establish whether the findings are reliable and valid. It’s 12 people, Polestar’s own cars, and Polestar is attaching a documentary series to it.
There’s also an awkward backdrop for US readers. As we reported in June, Polestar was barred from selling new cars in the US starting with the 2027 model year under the connected vehicle rule, even though the Polestar 4 is built in South Korea. The brand is now centering its plans on Europe, with the Formula 2030 concept previewing its next models .
Credit: Polestar
Electrek’s Take
This is a topic that has fascinated me for years. I’ve driven a lot of EVs, and the spec sheet tells me very little about whether I’ll enjoy one. Two cars with the same 0-60 mph time can feel completely different. One makes you grin. The other pins you to the seat and leaves you oddly numb.
The problem is that it’s genuinely hard to discuss. What feels like confidence to one driver feels like an overassisted steering rack to another. It’s different for everyone, and there’s basically no quantitative data on it, so the conversation ends up being reviewers, me included, trading adjectives.
So kudos to Polestar and Oxford for trying. Matching blink rate, pupil size and heart rate against steering effort and telemetry is a real attempt to connect the engineering to the experience, and I haven’t seen an automaker publish anything like it.
And it matters more now than ever. EVs turned acceleration into a commodity. Family crossovers do 0-60 mph in under 5 seconds. If everyone has the straight-line numbers, the difference comes down to how the car makes you feel, and right now most automakers are tuning that by gut.
I wouldn’t take 89.2 versus 67.7 to the bank. Twelve drivers isn’t a big sample, and nobody needed a study to tell them a 544 hp car is on average more fun than a 268 hp one. But the steering result and that “better driver than you are” quote get at what I think separates great performance cars from fast ones: they make you feel in control while you go faster.
What I’d love to see next is the bigger version with cars from different brands. Would a Model 3 Performance, an Ioniq 5 N and a Polestar 4 produce measurably different responses at the same lap times? That’s the study I want to read.

Leapmotor B05 Electric Hatchback To Be Produced in Spain at Stellantis Group's Zaragoza Plant
9 photos
Photo: Leapmotor
Now retailing at less than 20,000 euros in Spain, the B05 is good for nearly 300 miles on a full charge. Although sport utility vehicles are all the rage in the European Union and the United Kingdom right now, the full-electric hatchback from Leapmotor will soon join the B10 crossover at the Stellantis group's Zaragoza plant.
Leapmotor hasn't said when B05 production is scheduled to start in Zaragoza , how many will be produced on a yearly basis, or how many euros the project will require. For the time being, a confirmation is all that Leapmotor is willing to share with the media. A coupe-like compact that looks really nice when compared to the overly clinical Volkswagen ID.3 Neo, the newcomer is more than meets the eye.
The same can be said about Leapmotor's decision to expand production to Spain. For starters, the Chinese automaker helps the Stellantis plant bring its factory closer to Zaragoza's declared maximum yearly output. Stellantis, meanwhile, brings the infrastructure and manufacturing footprint that would otherwise take years and substantial investments if Leapmotor were to do it alone.
Chinese automakers need more than large shipping vessels and a distributor to make a difference in the European space. They need proper spare parts logistics, customer support, service facilities, and a way to build vehicles closer to the markets where Chinese brands intend to sell them. Better still, this arrangement helps Leapmotor dodge a very prohibitive European import tariff.
The joint venture with Stellantis went live in 2024, with the Franco-Italian-American partner holding 51 percent. Stellantis, therefore, controls the Chinese partner's export, sales, and manufacturing activities outside China. The joint venture had grown to more than 850 sales and service locations across Europe by May 2026, and the B05 cements said partnership.
Photo: Leapmotor Also worth noting, the commercial ambition of the Chinese party is easier to understand when you look at the B05's pricing information for the Spanish market. After including the 3,375-euro Plan Auto+ subsidy and 900 euros from energy-saving certificates, the starting price of the compact electric hatchback falls to a very reasonable 19,400 euros.
This offer applies to the entry LifePro version with the 56.2 kilowatt-hour battery. For maximum range, customers have to select the larger battery. In its case, Leapmotor claims 482 kilometers (299 miles) in the WLTP. If you feel like Stellantis got the short stick, bear in mind that its own electric vehicle push failed to compete against Chinese rivals.
Stellantis has openly stated that it wants to use Leapmotor's electric vehicle technologies and cost base to strengthen its own electrification plans, and B05 production in Spain will certainly help the group develop more affordable EVs across its core brands. Stellantis and Leapmotor laid out the former's ambition in May 2026, confirming that Stellantis could use Leapmotor International's ecosystem to improve EV production costs.
Joint purchasing will also prove useful. Combining demand gives Stellantis and Leapmotor a stronger position when negotiating supplier contracts, therefore resulting in cheaper supplied components. But wait, there's more! European supply chains can support resilience, helping the partners move new models to market a little bit faster.
Inside, the rear-drive B05 gets a large central touchscreen, 21 driver-assistance functions, seven airbags, and plenty more as standard. The higher Design grade sweetens the deal with heated front seats, a heated steering wheel, a panoramic sunroof, and 12-speaker audio as opposed to six for the Life trim level. All in all, not bad for a model that competes against the Volkswagen ID.3 Pro and Stellantis' very own Peugeot e-308 .

By Gavin van Marle
20 October 2026
APM Terminals is facing the prospect of losing control of the Omani deepsea transhipment hub of Salalah.
Salalah Port Service Company announced it had “received formal notification from the Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology, confirming that the existing concession agreements will not be extended beyond their contractual expiry date of 1 November 2028,” it said in a filing to the Muscat Stock Exchange.
It added: “The notification further states that the decision not to extend the concession agreement is final and unconditional. The board of directors will consider the notification and assess its potential impact on the company.
“The company will also engage with the relevant stakeholders as appropriate and will keep the market updated on any material developments.”
According to local reports, the ministry separately confirmed the decision, and added that the existing operator was expected to maintain operations at the port until the concession ends.
The port is managed by Maersk’s port operating subsidiary, APM Terminals, which holds a 30% stake in Salalah Port Service Co and signed a 30-year operating concession in 1996 on a build-operate-transfer basis.
Oman’s state-owned shipping and logistics firm, Asyad, holds a 20% stake, and the government’s Social Cohesion Fund holds 10%. The remaining 40% ownership is split between local and institutional investors, on a free float basis. According to the CapitalIQ platform, the largest institutional investor is the Soros fund management LLP, which has just under 20%.
The half-year financial results recorded revenues growing around 20%, to hit OR50.7m ($132m) with container traffic for the six months up 15%, due to a higher number of vessel calls, prompted by the outbreak of the US/Israel-Iran conflict and subsequent closure of the Hormuz straits.
However, profitability declined dramatically, due to the one-off cost of repairing a crane hit by an Iranian drone attack , as well as a 72% increase in fuel costs over the first half of 2025, and a requirement to increase terminal staff to handle the higher number of vessel calls, said CFO Farooq Zuberi.
He added that volumes for July and August were also “very strong”. This followed a 31% increase in throughput last year, when Salalah was established as one of the key hubs for the new Gemini network.
Container throughput reached 4.3m teu in 2025, up from 3.3m teu the previous year, aided by an expansion project which took annual handling capacity up to 6m teu.
Meanwhile, Salalah has become a key regional node for Maersk and Gemini partner Hapag-Lloyd, which have continually stressed the importance of “controlling” the main transhipment hubs in their joint network, and yesterday The Loadstar reported the port had won new calls on one of Gemini’s Asia-Mediterranean services that recently resumed Suez transits.
According to Xeneta’s eeSea liner database, Salalah hosts 18 container liner services, with only two – feeder services to the Horn of Africa operated separately by MSC and Greta Shipping – not featuring the involvement of Maersk or Hapag-Lloyd. The two carriers together represent the vast majority of the port’s container cargo.
This week’s decision gives them a two-year window to structure their network accordingly.
The Omani government has yet to announce whether it will hold a formal tender process to decide on a new concessionaire for the facility after November 2028.

By Alexander Whiteman
20 October 2026
Mining developments in sub-Saharan Africa are boosting the continent’s infrastructure, which supply chain operators have been crying out for, but significant gaps remain.
Data from the OECD shows more than $155bn will be required for upgrades in port, rail, and road infrastructure over the next decade if the sub-Sahara region “is to meet its potential”, but with multiple projects already under way, there are positive signs.
DHL Express Sub-Saharan Africa CEO Hennie Heymans told The Loadstar : “We’ve seen enormous improvement. If you go to Kenya, there’s an incredibly smooth new highway, which is partly what’s driving the growth in that economy.
“If you look at Ethiopia, it is building €15bn airport in Addis Ababa. Rwanda, one of the smallest countries, is building a €4bn airport. If you talk about Nigeria, you talk about Lagos and Abuja. We see fantastic improvements in infrastructure.”
And this investment is having real world logistics implications, with journeys between Nairobi and Addis Ababa, that previously took upwards of a week, down to 24 hours; while an eight-lane highway has dropped domestic journeys from four hours to mere minutes.
Much of the spur behind this has been new mining operations, necessitating the development of roads, port improvements, and services to support them.
Also, forwarders in the region believe the arrival of mining presents opportunities for developing trade in the region, with the growth of secondary cities around the sites set to lead to commercial centres and provoke new demand for logistics.
Mr Heymans is not naïve over the changes still needed, noting that “there is still an infrastructural deficit”, but he said it would be remiss not to recognise the level of improvement that has taken place over the past decade.

BYD’s new Seagull EV is now its cheapest electric car in China with 5-minute Flash Charging, and starts at under $10,000.
BYD’s second-generation Seagull EV price and range
The all-electric hatchback is BYD’s smallest, most affordable EV in China. Sold as the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini in Europe, the UK, and other global markets, the Seagull is among the world’s top-selling EVs.
For its second generation, BYD upgraded it with more interior space, its new Blade Battery 2.0 and 5-minute Flash Charging technology, and a few added premium extras.
The new Seagull EV is now on sale in China, starting at just 62,900 yuan, or about $9,500. That’s with BYD’s “Super Trade-in” promotion.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Regular prices start at 65,900 yuan ($9,900), which is still less than its predecessor. The first-gen Seagull EV normally cost 69,900 yuan ($10,500) without incentives.
BYD’s new Seagull EV is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000), without a trade-in.
The second-generation Seagull is 425 mm longer and has a 150 mm longer wheelbase than its predecessor. It now measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. It also gains another seat thanks to the added space, with room for five passengers.
Unlike the current model, which is front-wheel-drive, the new Seagull switches to rear-wheel-drive. The setup uses a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from the 55 kW (75 hp) that its predecessor offered.
BYD second-generation Seagull EV (Source: Zhang Zhuo)
To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.
Inside, BYD overhauled the interior with its latest in-car software and technology. The setup includes a larger 15.6″ center infotainment screen, a two-spoke steering wheel, a redesigned center console with smart storage, and added physical buttons.
BYD second-generation Seagull EV interior (Source: BYD)
All variants include the DiLink 150 smart cockpit and BYD’s 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system.
Buyers can upgrade to the optional DiPilot 300 system with God’s Eye B intelligent driving assistance. The upgraded system uses a roof-mounted LiDAR to offer ADAS features, including City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.
The front seats now include heating, ventilation, and massage functions. BYD added a few other premium extras, including ambient lighting, a 50W wireless phone charger, and smart storage.
With BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the new battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. A full recharge, or 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes. Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes 12 minutes to charge from 20% to 97%.
The new Seagull EV is available with two BYD Blade 2.0 LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh, providing CLTC ranges of 320 km (199 miles) and 420 km (261 miles), respectively.
After launching in China, BYD is expected to introduce the larger, upgraded version overseas, likely as the second-generation Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

Commercial truck enforcement operations across the U.S. have uncovered hundreds of safety violations , with authorities placing drivers and vehicles out of service for mechanical defects, unsafe driving and regulatory violations.
The enforcement operations underscore the range of violations inspectors continue to identify on U.S. highways, from improper lane use and speeding to equipment failures and driver disqualifications .
One of the largest recent operations took place along Interstate 40 near Flagstaff, Arizona, where state troopers and transportation officials conducted 263 inspections and 195 weight checks during a three-day enforcement blitz Oct. 6-8.
The Arizona Department of Public Safety said the operation resulted in 110 unsafe vehicles and drivers being removed from the state’s roadways.
The operation, part of the Arrive Alive Arizona commercial vehicle enforcement initiative, also resulted in 80 Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance decals being issued to trucks that met inspection requirements.
The Arizona enforcement effort was among several commercial vehicle safety operations conducted or reported in October across Arizona, California, North Dakota and Kentucky.
North Dakota inspectors uncover 494 violations
Federal, state and local authorities identified 494 violations during a commercial vehicle safety operation in Williston, North Dakota, according to the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration .
FMCSA reported the results Oct. 8, saying inspectors conducted 109 commercial vehicle inspections, including 20 hazardous materials checks.
The inspections uncovered 122 out-of-service violations and resulted in 47 enforcement actions, including 27 citations and 20 warnings.
The agency did not specify how many individual drivers or vehicles were placed out of service, and the 122 out-of-service violations should not be interpreted as the number of trucks or drivers removed from service.
Authorities identified 494 violations during a commercial vehicle safety operation in Williston, North Dakota, on Oct. 8. (Photo: FMCSA)
Enforcement results at a glance
The table separates out-of-service violations from the actual number of drivers and vehicles removed from service.
Location | Inspections | Violations / citations | Out-of-service findings
Flagstaff, Arizona | 263 | Not reported | 110 drivers and vehicles combined

Source: FMCSA, Arizona Department of Public Safety, California Highway Patrol, Garden Grove Police Department and Kentucky State Police, as compiled in the supplied enforcement roundup. The September 29 Arizona case and September Kentucky totals fall outside the October 2–20 operation period but were reported in October.
Arizona troopers find truck with inoperative brakes
In a separate Arizona enforcement action Oct. 8, a state trooper stopped a commercial truck on Interstate 10 near Bapchule after receiving reports that the vehicle was speeding, nearly striking other vehicles and failing to maintain its lane.
An Arizona Highway Patrol officer inspecting a commercial truck near Bapschule on Oct. 8 uncovered extensive mechanical defects. (Photo: AZ DPS)
The inspection uncovered extensive mechanical defects, including seven broken trailer crossmembers, approximately five feet of damaged lower rail, severed electrical wiring and improperly connected air lines.
Authorities said all of the trailer’s brakes were inoperative because of a severed air line. The driver also lacked a required logbook.
The driver and semitrailer were placed out of service.
In another Arizona case, a trooper stopped a commercial vehicle in the Phoenix area Sept. 29 after observing a missing mud flap and a driver who was not wearing a seat belt.
During the inspection, the trooper discovered that the driver’s logbook incorrectly showed him in sleeper-berth status while operating the truck.
Authorities also determined the driver did not possess a valid commercial driver’s license and was prohibited from operating a commercial vehicle after failing a previous drug test.
The driver was cited and placed out of service.
Arizona authorities also targeted commercial trucks violating lane restrictions along Interstate 10 in Pinal County on Oct. 8.
Troopers took enforcement action against five commercial vehicles traveling in the left lane of an active construction zone between Phoenix and Tucson, where trucks were required to remain in the right lane.
According to DPS, the trucks traveled in the restricted lane for distances ranging from 1.5 miles to more than four miles, disrupting traffic flow through the construction zone.
California enforcement sidelines 41 drivers and vehicles
California Highway Patrol officers conducted a commercial vehicle safety operation in the Newhall area Oct. 13, issuing 279 citations for violations that included mechanical defects, improper lane use, speeding and unauthorized freeway stops.
The operation resulted in 28 commercial vehicles and 13 drivers being placed out of service.
In Garden Grove, California, police conducted a separate commercial vehicle enforcement checkpoint Oct. 13.
Officers completed 90 inspections, identified 90 violations and issued 55 citations.
Nine vehicles were placed out of service, and eight were towed, according to the Garden Grove Police Department.
Meanwhile, CHP officers in Merced County conducted a coordinated commercial vehicle enforcement operation Oct. 8 following complaints about trucks speeding, traveling in improper lanes and making unsafe lane changes.
The operation involved CHP’s Merced Area office, the Chowchilla River Commercial Vehicle Enforcement Facility and the agency’s Central Division Mobile Road Enforcement team.
Authorities did not release inspection totals or citation figures for the Merced operation.
In another enforcement action, CHP officers cited a commercial truck driver Oct. 2 after observing a tractor-trailer traveling 71 mph northbound on U.S. Highway 101 near Bailard Avenue in Santa Barbara County.
Kentucky reports 612 commercial vehicle violations
The Kentucky State Police Commercial Vehicle Enforcement East Region reported conducting 1,030 commercial motor vehicle inspections during September across its 25-county jurisdiction.
According to results released Oct. 17, the inspections uncovered 612 violations and resulted in 79 vehicles being placed out of service.
The agency also conducted 119 hazardous materials inspections during the month.
Kentucky State Police said vehicles placed out of service must have identified safety defects corrected before returning to the road.
The enforcement findings nevertheless highlight the importance of vehicle maintenance, driver qualification checks and compliance with federal and state commercial vehicle safety regulations.

Image: Air Canada Cargo
By Alex Lennane
20 October 2026
Airlines are strengthening freighter links between Asia, Europe, and the Americas for winter, adding transatlantic flights, connections to Latin American manufacturing and distribution hubs, and capacity serving Asia’s technology exports.
Air Canada Cargo’s new 767-30F services to Amsterdam, Monterrey, and Panama City join selected US frequency increases from Lufthansa Cargo, a new Cairo link from Air France, and additional transpacific options from JAL and Cathay Cargo.
The additions come as forwarders renegotiate allocations ahead of the winter passenger timetable, when fewer flights on some routes reduce available belly capacity.
Air Canada is explicitly targeting that seasonal gap with its new Toronto-Amsterdam freighter service, which begins on 29 October with two weekly flights. Monterrey starts on 26 October with three weekly services, while Panama City begins on 25 October with up to two.
“The introduction of our freighters in Amsterdam is an important step in strengthening our European network,” said Matthieu Casey, MD, commercial – cargo.
“This gives us dedicated main-deck capacity at a time of year when transatlantic capacity is more constrained, helping us better serve customers in the Netherlands and across Europe, while creating opportunities to connect their cargo through our global network.”
The additions also provide more routing options between Europe and Latin America through Toronto, including onward connections to Quito, Lima, Bogotá, and Mexico City.
For forwarders, the timetable change can mean finding replacement space as airlines redistribute allocations.
One airfreight forwarder explained to The Loadstar last month: “You get the winter schedules maybe six, eight, ten weeks in advance, and then obviously you can start renegotiating your capacities.”
However, those negotiations amid competing forwarders vying for space.
“Sometimes they say, ‘hey, you have three pallets on that flight, now you can only have two’. And then you need to find space somewhere else.”
The forwarder described securing replacement capacity from Europe to the US as “a little bit of a challenge”. Asian procurement was less sensitive to the seasonal switch, he said, because of year-round block-space agreements.
Air Canada’s Mexican expansion comes as Washington eases restrictions on the airlines from its southern neighbour. Aeroméxico confirmed on 19 October that the US Department of Transportation had revoked its October 2025 order, restoring flexibility to consider new services and additional frequencies from Mexico City’s two airports, subject to regulatory requirements. The dispute had involved passenger slots and the forced relocation of US freighter operations.
Elsewhere, Lufthansa Cargo’s winter schedule, effective 25 October, offers 88 freighter routes serving 40 destinations, including up to 46 weekly rotations to 17 Asia-Pacific destinations.
Singapore joins its Frankfurt-Taipei rotation, creating another intra-Asian connection. Additional Taipei and Chengdu services, and its twice-weekly Frankfurt-Ho Chi Minh City-Shanghai-Los Angeles operation, carry over from summer.
Selected US gateways receive additional frequencies, taking Dallas/Fort Worth to four weekly services, Houston to three, and New York JFK to five.
Air France-KLM-Martinair Cargo, meanwhile, is adding three weekly Paris-Cairo B777F flights. Its Amsterdam-Seoul freighter operation will run three times a week – one standalone service and two combined with Hong Kong – increasing dedicated capacity on the route.
Both Air France and Lufthansa are shifting Mumbai freighter operations to Navi Mumbai, although they are gateway changes rather than additional capacity.
Technology demand is another influence on deployment. JAL cited generative AI, semiconductors, and investment in digital infrastructure in its winter cargo announcement.
Its offering includes a new twice-weekly Narita-Los Angeles 747 freighter codeshare with Atlas Air, launched on 2 October, alongside six weekly Narita-Chicago services with Kalitta Air, and two Narita-Luxembourg services with Cargolux. Its own 767 freighter timetable adds a weekly Narita-Dalian service.
Cathay Cargo has also linked additional Americas freighter capacity for the peak to growth in semiconductor and data-centre equipment shipments from Asia. It expects a leased A330 converted freighter in the fourth quarter, operated on its behalf by Air Hong Kong, to support regional general cargo demand.
Latin American perishables provide another source of demand. Emirates SkyCargo said this month it had introduced seven additional weekly South American freighter flights since March, including services to Buenos Aires, Bogotá, São Paulo, and Quito.
The changes come against a backdrop of demand outpacing capacity. IATA reported global cargo demand up 4.4% year on year in August, while capacity fell 0.1%. Asia-North America cargo capacity demand increased 13.2%.
There may be new connections – but there are also new charges. Air Canada Cargo will increase its airfreight carrier surcharge from 26 October, citing Middle East unrest and rising fuel prices, airport and enroute fees, and currency fluctuations.
For UK-origin shipments to Canada and the US North-east/Midwest, the charge rises from 15p to 19p/kg, an increase of almost 27%. For other destinations covered by its long-haul category, the fee rises from 29p to 36p/kg. The surcharge is assessed on gross weight, rather than chargeable weight, and applies across rate products, unless otherwise specified.
MSC Air Cargo raised its surcharge from $1.70 or €1.70 to $2.30 or €2.30 per chargeable kg from 16 October, an increase of approximately 35%, with currency determined by country of sale.
JAL’s Japan-origin long-haul fuel surcharge rose from ¥185 ($1.17) to ¥192/kg on the same date. Its latest calculation used Singapore jet fuel averaging $174.33 a barrel during the second half of last month.
The forwarder’s September assessment, nevertheless, anticipated a moderate seasonal increase rather than an exceptional peak.
“For sure, we do not expect a peak season with rates doubling or anything,” he said.

By Ian Putzger Americas correspondent
20 October 2026
The US Customs & Border Protection Agency (CBP) wants more data and earlier filing of imports valued at $2,500 or less.
The compliance deadline for such imports arriving by mail has been pushed back three months, however, which prompted speculation that Washington wants to avoid further consumer cost inflation before the mid-term elections next month.
The new regime has two components. Low-value shipments that arrive as cargo will continue to be processed under entry type 11 requirements. For those reaching the US through the international postal network, CBP has created a new entry type category – 13.
These changes are part of the regulatory framework modifications to accommodate Washington’s ‘Big Beautiful Bill’ of last year that ushered in the end of de minimis exemption for imports valued below $800. It shifted customs processing to informal entry channels as a temporary solution until the hard de minimis sunset on 1 July next year.
According to CBP, about 52.4m imports were registered as type 11 entries between 1 September last year and 31 May this year, while there were 24.4m entries for postal imports.
Under the new regime, type 11 entries have to be filed electronically upon, or before, arrival in the US, replacing current CBP requirement for filings within 15 days of arrival.
The new deadline gives cause for concern. A sampling of entries between September and November last year by CBP found more than half the type 11 imports would have missed the new deadline.
In addition, CBP wants filings to include the final deliver-to-party as a required data element, if it differs from the consignee.
Cargo owners, logistics providers, and customs brokers will have to scramble to ensure their traffic complies with the new type 11 requirements. Forwarder Sobel Network Shipping warned that, “for brands, 3PLs, cross-border carriers, and customs brokers, the era of lightweight clearance procedures for parcel freight has closed”, and added that proactive operational alignment was necessary to prepare for the new regime.
This will include system integration and EDI preparedness and upstream data integrity, as well as evaluating their volume exposure under planned informal bonding mandates, and building a partnership with an experienced licensed customs broker.
The new type 13 regulations end the possibility of paper entries, mandating electronic filing at arrival of the shipment, or earlier. In addition to existing requirements entries must include the shipper or sender, as well as the package tracking number, which also has to be included by the carrier on the inbound manifest.
As with type 11 entries, CBP has tightened the timeline for type 13 filings, which have to be made within 15 days before the agency considers a shipment ‘voluntarily abandoned’. So far, it has held shipments for 30 days before deeming them abandoned.
CBP acknowledged that the tighter timeline, combined with elevated requirements, carried the risk of some importers not receiving their shipments.
On top of these requirements, CBP plans to introduce bond requirements for certain categories of informal entries. According to the agency, this is intended to prevent the entry of illicit substances and equipment, to curb counterfeit goods and intellectual property infringement, and for the benefit of trade law compliance.
In an interesting twist, CBP pushed the compliance deadline for type 13 entries back to 20 January, from the planned implementation date of 22 October. This is meant to give customs brokers, importers, and the broader trade community time to adapt their systems and processes, and prevent clearance bottlenecks.
However, several observers have suggested a different likely reason for the delay: they argue it pushes the impact of the new rules into next year, well past the mid-term elections in early November.
The type 13 regime has caused alarm over likely higher prescription drug costs for US citizens who access cheaper medications from outside the US, primarily Canada. Patients’ advocates and industry groups have criticised this, and warned of possible disruption of medications ordered from the northern neighbour.
And the administration in Washington has cause to be nervous about consumer sentiment over higher prices. According to a recent report from the US Labor Department, prices continued to rise last month. Critics of the government have blamed the rise in inflation squarely on economic policies and the war on Iran; and the higher cost of living has been widely adopted as a pivotal theme in the upcoming elections.

For most of the last two decades, trucking could read the politics of its workforce fights along a familiar line, with one party broadly friendly to the independent contractor model and the other broadly skeptical of it, but according to the policy and legal experts who briefed an American Trucking Associations committee at the group’s recent conference, that map is being redrawn in a way that should make every fleet operator uneasy regardless of their own politics, because the pressure on how trucking classifies and uses its workforce is now coming from both sides of the aisle at once.
The headline numbers alone guarantee change. There are 36 gubernatorial elections in 2026, and 17 of those are effectively open seats where a governor is term-limited or retiring, which historically produces more movement. On the legislative side, 88 of the country’s 99 state legislative chambers are up for election. Layer in a round of midterm redistricting and a genuinely contested set of races, and the experts cautioned that the partisan landscape could shift more after this cycle than it has in several. For an industry whose labor rules are increasingly written at the state and local level, that is a lot of ground moving at once.
The States To Watch
The legal team from Scopelitis , which tracks this terrain closely for the industry, flagged a specific set of states where the outcomes carry the most potential to change the rules trucking operates under. On the legislative side, the ones to watch are Alaska, Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. On the gubernatorial side, the races that have settled into genuine toss-up status are Georgia, Nevada, Wisconsin, and Ohio, with Alaska, Arizona, Iowa, Michigan, Oregon, Florida, Kansas, and Texas also worth monitoring.
There is a reason the same handful of industrial and Upper Midwest states keep appearing. These are the places where the workforce-classification question is most actively contested, where a change in a governor’s office or a flip in a legislative chamber can move quickly from an election result to a new rule about who can be an independent contractor and who must be an employee.
The Realignment That Changes Everything
The deeper story, and the one the experts spent the most time on, is not which party controls what. It is a realignment inside both parties that is converging on the same place.
On the Republican side, a growing bloc of what the ATA’s Capitol Hill team described as pro-worker populist conservatives has emerged. The team was careful to draw a distinction that matters here. These members are pro-worker, not pro-labor. They are not endorsing the agenda of the labor unions. Rather, they are trying to win the votes of working-class Americans who feel the unions have abandoned them, and their instinct is skepticism of large corporations. The practical effect, though, is that this group has been unwilling to back legislation the trucking industry considers straightforward and business-friendly, and the team said the bloc now stretches well beyond the Rust Belt states where it started, with members from across the country.
That shift has already stalled the industry’s federal priorities. The Modern Worker Empowerment Act, which would amend federal labor law to replace the shifting multi-factor classification test with a single, stable common-law standard, is the industry’s attempt to end the whipsaw in which every change of administration flips the rules. It was introduced by Representative Kevin Kiley of California, a longtime ally on this issue, and it cleared its House committee only after the industry was asked to personally lobby multiple Republican members to secure a party-line vote. It then stalled in the Senate. A separate bill narrowing the joint-employer standard, the Save Local Business Act introduced by Representative James Comer, was pulled from the House floor when Republican leadership realized that roughly 20 of its own members would not support it.
On the Democratic side, the briefing described rising momentum from progressive and self-described democratic socialist members who are capitalizing on the same working-class frustration, including leadership challenges aimed at long-tenured members. The result is that pro-worker Republicans and pro-labor Democrats increasingly share mutual interest on certain labor policies, even as they compete for the same voters. The ATA team’s blunt prediction was that this convergence means there will be no federal legislative movement to lock in an industry-friendly classification standard, which leaves the uncertainty the industry most wants to end firmly in place.
It Is Fair To Note The Other Side
This is a contested policy debate, and it is worth stating the case that the industry’s critics make, because it explains why the realignment has teeth.
Worker advocates and many state lawmakers argue that the independent contractor model, as used across parts of the gig and logistics economy, can leave workers without the protections employees receive, from unemployment insurance to workers’ compensation, and that tightening classification or extending some benefits to contractors corrects a real imbalance. That view is driving developments like portable benefits, a concept gaining traction at the state level that would attach retirement, healthcare, or reserve-account benefits to the worker rather than the employer. The industry is not uniformly opposed to the idea, and the Scopelitis team noted that the design details decide everything, with voluntary, flexible models drawing far less industry objection than rigid, mandatory state-fund versions that failed in Hawaii and Washington. The point is not that one side is right, but that the political energy behind reclassification is now bipartisan enough that trucking cannot count on either party to simply hold the line.
The Regulatory Counterweight, And Why It Is Not Enough
There is some movement in the industry’s favor, but it illustrates exactly why elections matter so much. The Department of Labor is moving toward a clearer independent contractor rule built on two core factors, the level of control the hiring entity exercises and whether the worker has a genuine entrepreneurial opportunity for profit and loss. The industry expects that rule to be published late in 2026 with a 60-day implementation window, and it includes language favorable to trucking, such as clarifying that contract terms requiring compliance with the law and with health and safety rules do not count as the kind of control that destroys contractor status. The ATA has also petitioned the National Labor Relations Board to adopt a similar standard.
But a regulation is only as durable as the administration that writes it. This same rule has ping-ponged between administrations for years, which is precisely why the industry has been chasing a permanent legislative fix, and precisely why the stalling of that legislation matters. What an election can give, the next election can take back.
Where The Real Action Moves
The experts closed with a warning that the most consequential changes may not happen in Washington or even in state capitals at all. As state legislatures grow more lopsided and gridlocked, the action is shifting to administrative agencies and city and local councils, which can move fast and with less visibility. T hey pointed to delivery-protection measures advancing in New York City and Chicago, some of which would require last-mile deliveries to be performed by employees rather than contractors, and to New Jersey’s recently effective regulation consolidating the ABC test across a wide range of employment statutes. The caution for operators was direct. By the time you hear about a local rule, it is often already done, and it can reshape your labor model overnight.
Why It Matters
The usual assumption that trucking’s workforce rules swing cleanly with one party or the other no longer holds, because a pro-worker Republican bloc and a pro-labor Democratic bloc are converging on more scrutiny of the independent contractor model at the same time, which means the pressure on how fleets classify and deploy labor is likely to grow no matter who wins in 2026. For fleet and finance leaders, the takeaway is that uncertainty itself is now the planning constant, so the smart posture is to watch the specific state, agency, and local arenas where these rules are actually being written, and to build a workforce model that can withstand scrutiny under a tightening standard rather than betting on a friendly election to hold the status quo in place.
This article is based on presentations by Scopelitis attorneys and American Trucking Associations government affairs and regulatory staff at an ATA policy committee session, and reflects the political analysis and predictions presented there. Characterizations of pending legislation and political dynamics are as described by the presenters.

T hey pointed to delivery-protection measures advancing in New York City and Chicago, some of which would require last-mile deliveries to be performed by employees rather than contractors, and to New Jersey’s recently effective regulation consolidating the ABC test across a wide range of employment statutes.

The usual assumption that trucking’s workforce rules swing cleanly with one party or the other no longer holds, because a pro-worker Republican bloc and a pro-labor Democratic bloc are converging on more scrutiny of the independent contractor model at the same time, which means the pressure on how fleets classify and deploy labor is likely to grow no matter who wins in 2026.

source_document.body:
Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Defence Richard Marles and Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy announce the contract with Anduril Australia to acquire the Ghost Shark, an autonomous underwater vehicle, at Fleet Base East in Sydney, Australia on Sept 10, 2025. (Photo: Australian Department of Defence)
SINGAPORE — Australia has unveiled new underwater warfare payloads for its unmanned naval drones, some of which will be tested at the ongoing AUKUS Pillar II exercise in the US, according to the Australian Department of Defence.
The modular payloads will be integrated onto Anduril’s Ghost Shark and C2 Robotics’ Speartooth unmanned underwater vehicles as well as Ocius’s Bluebottle unmanned surface vessel (USV), the Australian DoD said in an announcement. The payloads will be used to remotely deliver supply caches, sea mines and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
“These technologies directly deliver on the Royal Australian Navy’s mission requirements and will contribute to enhanced undersea warfare capabilities, seabed operations, sea denial and the protection of critical undersea infrastructure,” said the Australian announcement.
The unveiling of the payloads comes five months after AUKUS partners Australia, the US and United Kingdom announced the signing of an agreement on the development of payloads for UUVs.
The payloads were unveiled at Anduril Australia’s facility in Sydney, where Australian Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy said that the minelaying module would be able to deploy 12 mines. Meanwhile, the UAV module payload can deploy Anduril’s Altius strike and reconnaissance UAV, he said.
“The Ghost Shark now has teeth and will have the ability to inflict damage on any potential adversary,” Conroy added.
Some of the payloads will be deployed during the ongoing Exercise Maritime Big Play Pacific in the US, per the announcement. An earlier Australian DoD release explains, “Maritime Big Play exercises help AUKUS partners develop common, open standards to speed up adoption of new technology and improve cooperation on complex missions.”
Separately, Conroy also revealed at Monday’s unveiling that the Ocius Bluebottle USV for the Royal Australian Navy (RAN) will be integrated with a “thin-lined towed array sonar” that can be used for Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW).
RAN chief Vice Adm. Matt Buckley said at the media conference that the development of the payload modules was “an important investment in autonomous and uncrewed maritime systems” and allows the RAN flexibility to adapt to different missions and requirements in the future.
“Given the vastness of our maritime geography, the ability to rapidly deliver uncrewed systems adds numbers to our fleets and complements our crews, ships and submarines.”
